Some of the storms produced damaging winds and numerous tornadoes.  Brief torrential rainfall was also observed with the stronger storm cells. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved into the mid-Atlantic late on September 8. Widespread showers and thunderstorms developed in a warm and humid air mass ahead of the front, moving into eastern Pennsylvania during the evening and early overnight hours. With instability waning after dark, much of the convection remained sub-severe. However, some instances of damaging wind did occur, particularly along a bowing line segment in Berks County. Showers and storms continued to gradually weaken as they shifted east later in the night.

A weak cold front dissipated west of the mid-Atlantic on June 4. However, a lingering surface trough slowly moved through the region. With a lingering warm and moist air mass in place, the surface trough caused convection to develop, starting early in the afternoon. Despite weak wind shear, storms steadily increased in organization, aided by favorable mesoscale interactions. Several storms would go on to pose a threat for damaging winds and hail. Storms eventually coalesced into multiple linear segments which posed a continued wind damage threat. Storms moved offshore by early to mid evening, with a drier air mass behind them.

A warm front moved through the mid-Atlantic on the morning of June 3. Considerable cloud cover lingered during and after the front passage, but breaks of sunshine gradually developed by afternoon. This, combined with a surge of moisture behind the warm front, allowed a moderate amount of instability to develop. A pre-frontal surface trough served as a focus for convective development by late afternoon. Convection became fairly widespread, but the moderate instability combined with only weak to moderate shear limited its overall severity, and the high moisture contributed to a messy convective evolution. A few reports of damaging wind were received, and storms also produced locally heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and wires were downed near Armorcrast Rd. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An advancing cold front, along with shortwave support, created the chance for thunderstorms across the region. Sufficient shear (40kts in the 0-6km layer), moderate to high instability (1500-2000 J/kg of CAPE), and dry mid-level air resulted in damaging winds and hail. Flash flooding occurred, mostly south of Pittsburgh, with training storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Nickel to quarter sized hail reported on social media.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large outflow boundary from a late night convective complex across northeast South Dakota and west central MN pushed southward, and interacted with a strong low-level jet. With steep mid-level lapse rates present, convective initiation resulted in intense updrafts along the boundary which produced large hail.

Heat and humidity led to strong instability by afternoon, as a weak frontal boundary settled into southeast South Dakota. Strong instability but weak deep-layer shear resulted in brief, intense and generally outflow-dominant storms.

The remnants of Hurricane Ida impacted the mid-Atlantic on September 1, 2021. As it moved northward, Ida began transitioning to a strong mid-latitude cyclone with pronounced frontal features, but with continued tropical moisture. On a regional level, the remnants of Ida became one of the most severe natural disasters in US history, due to a combination of several tornadoes, some of them strong, as well as catastrophic flooding over a large and densely populated area. The severe weather threat unfolded as the system's developing warm front lifted northward from the Delmarva region into Pennsylvania and New Jersey. South of the warm front, partial clearing and moderate to strong instability developed. Meanwhile, very strong shear and forcing, along with tropical moisture, were present within the warm sector. The result was widespread convection in the form of both supercell and quasi-linear thunderstorms. A number of storms became severe across the region, producing several tornadoes and other instances of wind damage. This continued an exceptionally active stretch of high end severe weather in the region, coming barely a month after the tornado outbreak of July 29.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The storm which produced a strong tornado in Montgomery County, |PA, cycled and produced another tornado in Bucks County, PA. |Damage began near in the area of Neshaminy Creek between Valley Rd|and Pebble Hill Rd in Doylestown. The tornado tracked north- |northeast from there, producing a consistent path of damage. |Damage was mainly confined to trees and was fairly extensive at |times, with much of the path length being heavily wooded. Numerous|hardwood and softwood trees were snapped and uprooted along the |path. Damage was strongly suggestive of tornadic winds, and a |tornado debris signature was also evident on radar. The heaviest |damage occurred near and along a stretch of Edison- Furlong Rd. |Extensive tree damage occurred along that road and a number of its|cross streets. Several utility poles were snapped in this area. |Tree damage along nearby Swamp Rd was also significant. The |tornado continued but began to lose intensity as it approached |Route 202, with sporadic tree damage observed on Mill Rd. Gradual |weakening continued and the tornado appeared to lift entirely in |the area of Burnt House Hill Rd. The extent of tree damage |suggested maximum winds of around 100 mph. No injuries were |reported as a result of this tornado.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With a move towards more near-normal temperatures and near-normal to above-normal precipitation for the month of July, drought status reductions from D2 - Severe Drought to D1 - Moderate Drought or D0 - Abnormally Dry were experienced across portions of central and western Iowa. While streamflow also remained below normal, improvement was experienced in many of the area streams and rivers.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A return to near-normal temperatures and near to above-normal precipitation allowed areas of central and western Iowa to see drought reductions from D2 - Severe Drought to D1 - Moderate Drought or D0 - Abnormally Dry conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Portions of central and western Iowa found themselves in a transition area of precipitation with areas to the north and east remaining below normal and areas to the south and west transitioning to near and above-normal amounts. Coupled with a return to near-normal temperatures, drought conditions receded within these counties by mid-July (July 13th Drought Monitor) and remained unchanged through the end of the month. Streamflow values largely remained well below normal in these areas as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A return to near-normal temperatures and lying within a transition zone of precipitation, ranging from continued below normal to the north and east to near and above-normal to the south and west, allowed some D2 - Severe Drought conditions to improve but not be eliminated throughout the county. D2 coverage was largely reduced by the July 13th issuance of the Drought Monitor, and remained stable through the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm tracked across the Upper Midwest from December 10th into the 11th. The storm brought snow and strong winds to parts of northeast Iowa. Snowfall amounts of 3 to 5 inches were common across Mitchell and Howard Counties. Extensive drifting of the snow occurred as gusts of 30 to 40 mph occurred during the early morning hours of the 11th. The highest reported snowfall total was 5.6 inches in St Ansgar (Mitchell County).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Portions of central and western Iowa found themselves in a transition area of precipitation with areas to the north and east remaining below normal and areas to the south and west transitioning to near and above-normal amounts. Coupled with a return to near-normal temperatures, drought conditions receded within these counties by mid-July (July 13th Drought Monitor) and remained unchanged through the end of the month. Streamflow values largely remained well below normal in these areas as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A return to near-normal temperatures and lying within a transition zone of precipitation, ranging from continued below normal to the north and east to near and above-normal to the south and west, allowed some D2 - Severe Drought conditions to improve but not be eliminated throughout the county. D2 coverage was largely reduced by the July 13th issuance of the Drought Monitor, and remained stable through the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Heavy rain brought localized flooding to Fulton County on Sunday April 11th.  Flooding on Licking Creek in Needmore, PA resulted in one fatality when a man drove over a flooded bridge.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rain resulted in flooding on Licking Creek. A man crossing a flooded road, was swept away, and was later found deceased.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An isolated supercell developed behind a southward sagging frontal boundary.  With around 1000 J/kg MLCAPE and 40-45 knots of effective shear, a brief supercellular structure evolved. Even with hail size somewhat limited by available instability, substantial damage to total destruction of crops occurred due to the large quantity of wind-driven hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind-driven hail produced considerable to total crop damage. Damage began around 4 miles southeast of Le Mars, and followed a nearly continuous 1 to 3 mile wide path for 17 miles to the southeast, crossing into Cherokee and Woodbury County around 6 miles east southeast of Kingsley.  Hail varied from dime to quarter size along the path, with quarter size hail 3 miles north northeast of Kingsley at 1734 CST and 5 miles east northeast of Kingsley at 1738 CST.  Winds were estimated as high as 60 to 65 mph. Damage was done to the siding of a house 1.5 miles east of O Leary at 1720 CST.  The worst crop damage occurred from 3 miles north to 4 miles east of Kingsley, where hail was still 3 inches deep on roadways an hour after the storm.  The path was determined from surface reports and Sentinel satellite data. Crop damage is an estimate from insured losses. Information provided by the United States Department of Agriculture. Property damage costs are a rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms developed ahead of an approaching cold front during the afternoon and evening of Wednesday, July 14.  Some of the storms produced damaging winds and numerous tornadoes.  Brief torrential rainfall was also observed with the stronger storm cells.  The areas that were hit hardest were in Buchanan, Delaware, Benton, Linn, and Jones counties in IA, where a total of 14 tornadoes occurred.  7 of the tornadoes had no visible damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado briefly touched down on the southwest side of town damaging several farm outbuildings and a large show barn. No injuries were reported.

The tornado was seen briefly by the resident before seeking shelter. A business on the southeast side of Neola also had substantial damage to large metal buildings, at least two of which were destroyed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A few supercell thunderstorms developed ahead of a warm front advancing into the forecast area, where they produced gusty winds, heavy rain, and hail up to 3 inches in diameter. Storms initially developed as more discrete supercells early in the evening, with the storm that went through Burlington being one of the more intense storms. Rainfall amounts reached 2 inches or more in some areas, as the anomalously moist environment favored excessive rainfall that lead to flash flooding. The La Moine River near Colmar also raised to Minor Flood stage due to the heavy rain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Tropical Storm Elsa approached the mid-Atlantic states from the south on July 8. Downstream of Elsa, a warm and moist environment was present. A slow moving frontal boundary also resided over northern New Jersey, northern Pennsylvania, and into New York. This frontal system provided forcing for convective development over the mid-Atlantic, in fairly close proximity but unrelated to Tropical Storm Elsa. With strong instability and weak to moderate wind shear, some of the storms became severe as they organized into linear and multi-cellular clusters. Deep layer southerly flow in advance of Elsa caused storms to move northward as opposed to a more typical eastward motion. Damaging wind was the main hazard associated with these storms, with several strong downbursts noted. Storm activity eventually weakened and moved north of the region by evening as Elsa moved in.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front moved through the mid-Atlantic on the morning of June 3. Considerable cloud cover lingered during and after the front passage, but breaks of sunshine gradually developed by afternoon. This, combined with a surge of moisture behind the warm front, allowed a moderate amount of instability to develop. A pre-frontal surface trough served as a focus for convective development by late afternoon. Convection became fairly widespread, but the moderate instability combined with only weak to moderate shear limited its overall severity, and the high moisture contributed to a messy convective evolution. A few reports of damaging wind were received, and storms also produced locally heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few reports of tree limbs and power lines down north and northeast of New Morgan. Time estimated from radar.

Hot and humid conditions existed over the mid-Atlantic on July 6, with a cold front well northwest over the Great Lakes and southern Canada. As temperatures rose into the 90s with dew points in the upper 60s and low 70s, strong instability built over the region. A pre-frontal trough and a fast moving upper level disturbance provided some lift, which helped convection develop by mid afternoon. Convection was initially concentrated over northern Pennsylvania and New York, near the better forcing, but propagated southeastward with time. Shear was weak to moderate but sufficient to allow some storm organization into multi-cellular and linear segments. A number of storms became severe, producing damaging winds and some hail. As storms moved southeast, outflow boundaries moving even further south helped ignite additional convection, some severe, which continued into the early overnight hours. The early overnight convection was also noted to be especially prolific with regard to lightning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree fell and other branches and limbs were downed in the area from a likely downburst. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure developed over the northern Gulf of Mexico on the morning of February 15 and moved northeast into the Tennessee and Ohio River Valleys through the afternoon and evening hours. Well ahead of this low pressure system, a band of snow overspread the region with a weak front during the morning hours of the 15th, allowing for a quick inch or two of snow across the area. As the low crept closer to the region, deepening over the Ohio/Pennsylvania border and bringing ample Gulf moisture into the region, a broader area of precipitation moved through the area during the afternoon and evening hours. For Northwest Pennsylvania, this precipitation started in the form of sno, but by evening, a nose of warmer air just above the surface allowed for snow to melt and for the end precipitation type to become a mix of sleet and freezing rain significantly lessening snowfall amounts in several locations. Behind the low pressure system, colder air surged into the region and lake effect snow developed over Lake Erie and entered Northeast Ohio on the 16th. By the late evening of the 16th, an additional 4 to 8 inches of snow fell in portions of the snow belt, adding to the wintry mix from the night before. Impacts were mixed in Northwest Pennsylvania as the first half of the event underperformed but the lake effect on the 16th overperformed, leading to mixed preparedness for the region. For the entire event, the highest total snowfall measurement in Pennsylvania was 11 inches by a trained snow spotter northwest of Edinboro in south central Erie County. Erie International Airport only recorded 2.8 inches of snow for this event. There were no known injuries or fatalities in Northwest Pennsylvania on account of this winter storm.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Three rounds of snow moved through Northwest Pennsylvania on February 15 and 16. The first round on the morning of the 15th brought a quick inch of snow to the region. A second round of snow entered during the afternoon and evening hours, bringing an additional 1 to 4 inches of snow to the region. For a brief period during the evening of the 15th, snow transitioned to sleet and freezing rain, as some warmer air aloft melted the snow but near surface temperatures below freezing allowed for wintry precipitation to continue. Sleet amounts of a few tenths and ice amounts up to one tenth were observed across the area. A third round of snow came in the form of lake effect snow and an additional 1 to 3 inches of snow fell. Total snowfall for the event for the northern portions of Erie County ranged from roughly 3 to 9 inches of snow. The maximum snowfall for this event was in Spring Township, where a trained snow spotter measured 10 inches of snow for the event. Other selected snowfall totals for the event include: 6 inches in Meadville, 5 inches in Springboro, 4 inches northwest of Jamestown, and 3.6 inches in Atlantic.

A western upper level trough underwent lee cyclogenesis over the central Rockies and into the central Plains. Strong moisture transport out of the Gulf region and from the pacific northwest into the system with strong lift within the dendritic growth zone made for periods of moderate to heavy snow with rates exceeding an inch per hour. Precipitation began with a very narrow window of drizzle before transitioning over to snow behind the cold front. Strong winds behind the front gusted over 40 mph behind the front, resulting in blizzard or near blizzard conditions across much of northern and into central Iowa. The high shear also allowed for the development of horizontal convective rolls over northern Iowa, causing rapid reductions in visibility within the rolls. A number of car accidents occurred due to reduced visibility and slick road conditions including two multi car pile ups. A 30 car pile up in Jasper county and a 10 car pile up in Polk county. Non-traditional sources such as impacts, webcams, and spotter reports, were evaluated to classify this event as a Blizzard over rural areas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure developed over the northern Gulf of Mexico on the morning of February 15 and moved northeast into the Tennessee and Ohio River Valleys through the afternoon and evening hours. Well ahead of this low pressure system, a band of snow overspread the region with a weak front during the morning hours of the 15th, allowing for a quick inch or two of snow across the area. As the low crept closer to the region, deepening over the Ohio/Pennsylvania border and bringing ample Gulf moisture into the region, a broader area of precipitation moved through the area during the afternoon and evening hours. For Northwest Pennsylvania, this precipitation started in the form of sno, but by evening, a nose of warmer air just above the surface allowed for snow to melt and for the end precipitation type to become a mix of sleet and freezing rain significantly lessening snowfall amounts in several locations. Behind the low pressure system, colder air surged into the region and lake effect snow developed over Lake Erie and entered Northeast Ohio on the 16th. By the late evening of the 16th, an additional 4 to 8 inches of snow fell in portions of the snow belt, adding to the wintry mix from the night before. Impacts were mixed in Northwest Pennsylvania as the first half of the event underperformed but the lake effect on the 16th overperformed, leading to mixed preparedness for the region. For the entire event, the highest total snowfall measurement in Pennsylvania was 11 inches by a trained snow spotter northwest of Edinboro in south central Erie County. Erie International Airport only recorded 2.8 inches of snow for this event. There were no known injuries or fatalities in Northwest Pennsylvania on account of this winter storm.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Three rounds of snow moved through Northwest Pennsylvania on February 15 and 16. The first round on the morning of the 15th brought a quick inch of snow to the region. A second round of snow entered during the afternoon and evening hours, bringing an additional 2 to 5 inches of snow to the region. For a brief period during the evening of the 15th, snow transitioned to sleet and freezing rain, as some warmer air aloft melted the snow but near surface temperatures below freezing allowed for wintry precipitation to continue. Sleet amounts of a few tenths and ice amounts up to one tenth were observed across the area. A third round of snow came in the form of lake effect snow and an additional 1 to 3 inches of snow fell. Total snowfall for the event for the northern portions of Erie County ranged from roughly 3 to 9 inches of snow. The maximum snowfall for this event was in the city of Erie, where a trained snow spotter measured 9.4 inches of snow for the event. Other selected snowfall totals for the event include: 9 inches in Lake City, 8.4 inches in North East, 6.9 inches in Harborcreek, and 2.8 inches at Erie International Airport.

A number of car accidents occurred due to reduced visibility and slick road conditions including two multi car pile ups. A 30 car pile up in Jasper county and a 10 car pile up in Polk county. Non-traditional sources such as impacts, webcams, and spotter reports, were evaluated to classify this event as a Blizzard over rural areas.

A line of storms that developed over western Nebraska and South Dakota moved into a highly unstable airmass with 2500-3000 J/kg MLCAPE leading to widespread wind damage across eastern Nebraska and western Iowa. According to the Omaha Public Power District, nearly 200,000 customers were without power.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Iowa mesonet site measured a peak wind gust of 62 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A long-duration winter storm produced widespread snowfall across central Pennsylvania from January 31 to February 2, 2021. Although the snow began on January 31st, warning criteria was not met in any central Pennsylvania counties until February 1st or 2nd. Widespread snowfall amounts of 10-15 inches were observed, with more than 20 inches of accumulation in portions of Schuylkill County. This was a Miller Type B storm, with the primarily low pushing up the Ohio Valley before a center-jump to the Mid-Atlantic coast was observed. Snow was the predominant precipitation type, although the Lower Susquehanna Valley had a several hour period of light wintry mix before the coastal low strengthened. The system then very slowly pulled east-northeastward along the southern New England coast and out to sea.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A winter storm produced 9 to 11 inches of snow across northern Lycoming County from January 31 to February 2, 2021.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Portions of northeast Iowa suffered through blizzard conditions during the afternoon of February 4th. A storm system produced 3 to 5 inches of snow along with winds of 35 to 45 mph that reduced the visibility to under a quarter mile for a few hours and drifted roads shut with travel not advised across the region for much of the afternoon. The automated weather observing equipment at both the Charles City (Floyd County) and Oelwein (Fayette County) airports reported 4 to 5 hours when the visibility was reduced to a quarter mile or less by falling and blowing snow. Most schools canceled classes for the day because of the storm. The highest reported snowfall amount was 5 inches around New Hampton (Chickasaw County) and the highest recorded wind gust was 44 mph by the automated weather observing equipment at the Oelwein airport.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: COOP and volunteer observers reported that around 4 inches of snow fell across Clayton County. Roads across the county became snow covered and travel was not advised at times during the afternoon. Several schools across the county canceled classes for the day. The highest reported snowfall amount was 4.1 inches southwest of Elkader.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Following a more than two week stretch of dry weather, a cold front approached the mid-Atlantic on May 26. Ahead of the front, an unseasonably hot and humid air mass developed, with high temperatures near to above 90 degrees in much of the region. This contributed to strong instability, while wind shear was more moderate. Multiple rounds of convection affected the region, triggered by a pre-frontal trough and a couple of upper level impulses ahead of the front. A fairly widespread severe weather event resulted, with damaging winds by far the most widespread hazard. Numerous instances of downed trees and power lines and some property damage were reported. Thunderstorms during the evening hours were also prolific lightning producers. The final round of storms finally moved offshore close to midnight after several hours of severe weather in the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and wires were downed near Sixth St and Market St. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A moisture-laden system developed over the Gulf States and pushes up the spine of the Appalachians, bring a wintry mix of snow, sleet and freezing rain to central Pennsylvania from the evening of February 15 into the morning of February 16. The Lower Susquehanna Valley quickly went over to plain rain after a brief period of freezing rain, while the central mountains had a prolonged period of sleet and freezing rain with many locations receiving over 0.25 of ice accretion. North of I-80, there was 1-2 inches of snow and sleet followed by freezing rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A winter storm produced a quarter of an inch of ice accumulation, plus half an inch of sleet and 2 inches of snow to Elk County from February 15-16, 2021.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A moisture-laden system developed over the Gulf States and pushes up the spine of the Appalachians, bring a wintry mix of snow, sleet and freezing rain to central Pennsylvania from the evening of February 15 into the morning of February 16. The Lower Susquehanna Valley quickly went over to plain rain after a brief period of freezing rain, while the central mountains had a prolonged period of sleet and freezing rain with many locations receiving over 0.25 of ice accretion. North of I-80, there was 1-2 inches of snow and sleet followed by freezing rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A winter storm produced a quarter of an inch of ice accumulation, plus half an inch of sleet and an inch of snow across northern Lycoming County from February 15-16, 2021.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A massive arctic plunge into the Northern Plains brought almost a week of dangerous and life threatening wind chills to the region. The worst conditions were recorded between February 13 and February 16 when wind chills occasionally dropped as low as 35 below to 55 below zero. Numerous record low maximum and minimum temperatures were also established. The areal extent of the extreme cold in the central portions of the U.S. led to stress on the power grid, which necessitated several short-term rolling power outages impacting more than 10,000 customers during the peak of the cold.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: During several periods over three days with wind chill below -35, values reached a minimum of -42 at Ida Grove.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A quick moving upper level wave amplified while sliding eastward across the Central Plains.  Snowfall developed quickly ahead of this feature, with broad snowfall in and near northwest Iowa collapsing into a narrow band due to the presence of mid-level instability above a lower-level frontogenetic zone.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall reduced visibility to one-quarter to one-half mile at times between 0700-1200CST and produced treacherous travel conditions. Accumulation reached 8.0 inches 4 miles north northeast of Hornick, 6.5 inches 1 mile east of Bronson and 6.0 inches at Sergeant Bluff.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A long-duration winter storm produced widespread snowfall across central Pennsylvania from January 31 to February 2, 2021. Although the snow began on January 31st, warning criteria was not met in any central Pennsylvania counties until February 1st or 2nd. Widespread snowfall amounts of 10-15 inches were observed, with more than 20 inches of accumulation in portions of Schuylkill County. This was a Miller Type B storm, with the primarily low pushing up the Ohio Valley before a center-jump to the Mid-Atlantic coast was observed. Snow was the predominant precipitation type, although the Lower Susquehanna Valley had a several hour period of light wintry mix before the coastal low strengthened. The system then very slowly pulled east-northeastward along the southern New England coast and out to sea.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A winter storm produced 11 to 14 inches of snow across Sullivan County from January 31 to February 2, 2021.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Following a more than two week stretch of dry weather, a cold front approached the mid-Atlantic on May 26. Ahead of the front, an unseasonably hot and humid air mass developed, with high temperatures near to above 90 degrees in much of the region. This contributed to strong instability, while wind shear was more moderate. Multiple rounds of convection affected the region, triggered by a pre-frontal trough and a couple of upper level impulses ahead of the front. A fairly widespread severe weather event resulted, with damaging winds by far the most widespread hazard. Numerous instances of downed trees and power lines and some property damage were reported. Thunderstorms during the evening hours were also prolific lightning producers. The final round of storms finally moved offshore close to midnight after several hours of severe weather in the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and wires were downed near Chapel Hill Rd. Time estimated from radar.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: SNOW SQUALL. A snow squall on the leading edge of a mesoscale band of heavy snow briefly dropped visibility to under one quarter mile in and produced flash-freeze conditions in eastern Synder County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Following a more than two week stretch of dry weather, a cold front approached the mid-Atlantic on May 26. Ahead of the front, an unseasonably hot and humid air mass developed, with high temperatures near to above 90 degrees in much of the region. This contributed to strong instability, while wind shear was more moderate. Multiple rounds of convection affected the region, triggered by a pre-frontal trough and a couple of upper level impulses ahead of the front. A fairly widespread severe weather event resulted, with damaging winds by far the most widespread hazard. Numerous instances of downed trees and power lines and some property damage were reported. Thunderstorms during the evening hours were also prolific lightning producers. The final round of storms finally moved offshore close to midnight after several hours of severe weather in the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed on Basket Rd. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved into the mid-Atlantic late on September 8. Widespread showers and thunderstorms developed in a warm and humid air mass ahead of the front, moving into eastern Pennsylvania during the evening and early overnight hours. With instability waning after dark, much of the convection remained sub-severe. However, some instances of damaging wind did occur, particularly along a bowing line segment in Berks County. Showers and storms continued to gradually weaken as they shifted east later in the night.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed onto a garage. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A fast moving arctic cold front brought dangerous conditions to portions of the area. Rain, mixed with freezing rain and sleet moved into eastern Iowa during the early morning, then as a cold front moved in from the west during the mid morning, the rain switched to snow. Strong winds and falling temperatures behind the front caused wet roads to quickly freeze.  Snow fell for several hours after the change over and became heavy at times, with widespread 2 to 6 inches of snowfall. Winds behind the front were 25 to 35 mph with gusts up to 45 mph during the afternoon and evening causing blowing snow in open areas. Whiteout conditions were seen in open areas, and some areas experienced periods of near blizzard conditions, especially across east central and  northeast Iowa. Significant drifting snow continued into Feb. 5.  Wind chills dropped to 5 below to 15 below zero late Thursday night and Friday morning along and north of I-80.||Key impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents, and road closures.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Rain and wintry mix started the day, leading to snow (heavy at times), where between 2 and 5 inches of snow fell throughout Clinton County. Strong winds were also noted in the afternoon, with a peak gust at 45 mph reported at the Clinton Airport AWOS.

A strong band of heavy snow began to develop along the northwest side of the low as it tracked northeast. The lift and moisture available was enough to create an area of intensification along the front which resulted in some areas receiving around 2 to 3 inches per hour snowfall rates. As a result, some locations in Ohio had over achieving snowfall amounts that went over 6 inches in some instances.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A fast moving arctic cold front brought dangerous conditions to portions of the area. Rain, mixed with freezing rain and sleet moved into eastern Iowa during the early morning, then as a cold front moved in from the west during the mid morning, the rain switched to snow. Strong winds and falling temperatures behind the front caused wet roads to quickly freeze.  Snow fell for several hours after the change over and became heavy at times, with widespread 2 to 6 inches of snowfall. Winds behind the front were 25 to 35 mph with gusts up to 45 mph during the afternoon and evening causing blowing snow in open areas. Whiteout conditions were seen in open areas, and some areas experienced periods of near blizzard conditions, especially across east central and  northeast Iowa. Significant drifting snow continued into Feb. 5.  Wind chills dropped to 5 below to 15 below zero late Thursday night and Friday morning along and north of I-80.||Key impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents, and road closures.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Following a more than two week stretch of dry weather, a cold front approached the mid-Atlantic on May 26. Ahead of the front, an unseasonably hot and humid air mass developed, with high temperatures near to above 90 degrees in much of the region. This contributed to strong instability, while wind shear was more moderate. Multiple rounds of convection affected the region, triggered by a pre-frontal trough and a couple of upper level impulses ahead of the front. A fairly widespread severe weather event resulted, with damaging winds by far the most widespread hazard. Numerous instances of downed trees and power lines and some property damage were reported. Thunderstorms during the evening hours were also prolific lightning producers. The final round of storms finally moved offshore close to midnight after several hours of severe weather in the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and wires were downed near Hillcrest Rd. Time estimated from radar.

Rain, mixed with freezing rain and sleet moved into eastern Iowa during the early morning, then as a cold front moved in from the west during the mid morning, the rain switched to snow. Strong winds and falling temperatures behind the front caused wet roads to quickly freeze.  Snow fell for several hours after the change over and became heavy at times, with widespread 2 to 6 inches of snowfall. Winds behind the front were 25 to 35 mph with gusts up to 45 mph during the afternoon and evening causing blowing snow in open areas. Whiteout conditions were seen in open areas, and some areas experienced periods of near blizzard conditions, especially across east central and  northeast Iowa. Significant drifting snow continued into Feb. 5.  Wind chills dropped to 5 below to 15 below zero late Thursday night and Friday morning along and north of I-80.||Key impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents, and road closures.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Rain and wintry mix started the day, leading to snow (heavy at times), where between 3 and 4 inches of snow fell throughout the county, with a peak wind gust of 43 mph observed at the Independence AWOS. Blizzard conditions were noted through mid to late afternoon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A long-duration winter storm produced widespread snowfall across central Pennsylvania from January 31 to February 2, 2021. Although the snow began on January 31st, warning criteria was not met in any central Pennsylvania counties until February 1st or 2nd. Widespread snowfall amounts of 10-15 inches were observed, with more than 20 inches of accumulation in portions of Schuylkill County. This was a Miller Type B storm, with the primarily low pushing up the Ohio Valley before a center-jump to the Mid-Atlantic coast was observed. Snow was the predominant precipitation type, although the Lower Susquehanna Valley had a several hour period of light wintry mix before the coastal low strengthened. The system then very slowly pulled east-northeastward along the southern New England coast and out to sea.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A winter storm produced 8 to 12 inches of snow across Adams County from January 31 to February 2, 2021.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Following a more than two week stretch of dry weather, a cold front approached the mid-Atlantic on May 26. Ahead of the front, an unseasonably hot and humid air mass developed, with high temperatures near to above 90 degrees in much of the region. This contributed to strong instability, while wind shear was more moderate. Multiple rounds of convection affected the region, triggered by a pre-frontal trough and a couple of upper level impulses ahead of the front. A fairly widespread severe weather event resulted, with damaging winds by far the most widespread hazard. Numerous instances of downed trees and power lines and some property damage were reported. Thunderstorms during the evening hours were also prolific lightning producers. The final round of storms finally moved offshore close to midnight after several hours of severe weather in the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed on Reifsnyder Rd near Swamp Picnic Rd. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very strong cold front was accompanied by a narrow band of moderate to heavy snowfall, as well as wind gusting to 30 to 45 mph.  Most areas saw a brief period of rain, freezing rain or sleet before changing to snow, which was accompanied by a temperature fall of 10 to 20 degrees over a six hour period.  Contraction of the band occurred due to strong elevated instability, with isolated thunder occurring in southeast South Dakota and southwest Minnesota.  While most areas received around an inch or two of snowfall, the band peaked in intensity around the Sioux Falls area with up to three to five inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: After a brief period of light freezing rain, snowfall was briefly heavy and totaled 1.6 inches 3 miles west northwest of Everly and 1.2 inches at Spencer. Roads became hazardous, and frequent wind gusts as high as 41 mph at Spencer produced several hours of blowing snow with visibility as low as one-half mile.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the morning of January 31st, weakening low pressure moved northward into the lower Ohio Valley. Frontogenetic forcing allowed for some higher snow rates during the morning and early afternoon hours, particularly in the higher elevations. Snow rates became lighter in the afternoon as support for lift weakened and lifted northward, and as energy began to transfer to a coastal low. Accumulations through midnight were generally limited to four inches or less. ||This event continued into early February, when strengthening northwest flow increased cold advection and allowed additional accumulating snow showers to develop.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Average storm total snowfall in the ridges of Westmoreland County from Jan 31st to Feb 3rd was 8 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Runoff from the heavy rain associated with Post Tropical Cyclone Ida produced moderate to major flooding along the tidal Delaware River on the night of September 1.  There was another round of moderate flooding on the night of September 2.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Major flooding occurred along the tidal Delaware River and its tidal tributaries in lower Bucks County, inundating adjacent roadways and properties.  The tide gauge at Newbold, Pennsylvania reached a record level of 13.22 feet Mean Lower Low Water.  The tide gauge at Burlington, New Jersey tied its record level of 11.94 feet Mean Lower Low Water.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Portions of northeast Iowa suffered through blizzard conditions during the afternoon of February 4th. A storm system produced 3 to 5 inches of snow along with winds of 35 to 45 mph that reduced the visibility to under a quarter mile for a few hours and drifted roads shut with travel not advised across the region for much of the afternoon. The automated weather observing equipment at both the Charles City (Floyd County) and Oelwein (Fayette County) airports reported 4 to 5 hours when the visibility was reduced to a quarter mile or less by falling and blowing snow. Most schools canceled classes for the day because of the storm. The highest reported snowfall amount was 5 inches around New Hampton (Chickasaw County) and the highest recorded wind gust was 44 mph by the automated weather observing equipment at the Oelwein airport.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A winter storm dropped 3 to 4 inches of snow across Floyd County. A period of blizzard conditions occurred in the afternoon when winds gusted to between 35 and 40 mph and the combination of falling and blowing snow reduced the visibility to a quarter mile or less. Travel was not advised as roads were completely snow covered and some were closed by drifts. Most schools across the county canceled classes for the day. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A massive arctic plunge into the Northern Plains brought almost a week of dangerous and life threatening wind chills to the region. The worst conditions were recorded between February 13 and February 16 when wind chills occasionally dropped as low as 35 below to 55 below zero. Numerous record low maximum and minimum temperatures were also established. The areal extent of the extreme cold in the central portions of the U.S. led to stress on the power grid, which necessitated several short-term rolling power outages impacting more than 10,000 customers during the peak of the cold.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: During several periods over three days with wind chill below -35, values reached a minimum of -44 at Beaver Creek and -42 at Sheldon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A fast moving arctic cold front brought dangerous conditions to portions of the area. Rain, mixed with freezing rain and sleet moved into eastern Iowa during the early morning, then as a cold front moved in from the west during the mid morning, the rain switched to snow. Strong winds and falling temperatures behind the front caused wet roads to quickly freeze.  Snow fell for several hours after the change over and became heavy at times, with widespread 2 to 6 inches of snowfall. Winds behind the front were 25 to 35 mph with gusts up to 45 mph during the afternoon and evening causing blowing snow in open areas. Whiteout conditions were seen in open areas, and some areas experienced periods of near blizzard conditions, especially across east central and  northeast Iowa. Significant drifting snow continued into Feb. 5.  Wind chills dropped to 5 below to 15 below zero late Thursday night and Friday morning along and north of I-80.||Key impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents, and road closures.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A long-duration winter storm produced widespread snowfall across central Pennsylvania from January 31 to February 2, 2021. Although the snow began on January 31st, warning criteria was not met in any central Pennsylvania counties until February 1st or 2nd. Widespread snowfall amounts of 10-15 inches were observed, with more than 20 inches of accumulation in portions of Schuylkill County. This was a Miller Type B storm, with the primarily low pushing up the Ohio Valley before a center-jump to the Mid-Atlantic coast was observed. Snow was the predominant precipitation type, although the Lower Susquehanna Valley had a several hour period of light wintry mix before the coastal low strengthened. The system then very slowly pulled east-northeastward along the southern New England coast and out to sea.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A winter storm produced 9 to 16 inches of snow across Lancaster County from January 31 to February 2, 2021.

Ahead of the front, an unseasonably hot and humid air mass developed, with high temperatures near to above 90 degrees in much of the region. This contributed to strong instability, while wind shear was more moderate. Multiple rounds of convection affected the region, triggered by a pre-frontal trough and a couple of upper level impulses ahead of the front. A fairly widespread severe weather event resulted, with damaging winds by far the most widespread hazard. Numerous instances of downed trees and power lines and some property damage were reported. Thunderstorms during the evening hours were also prolific lightning producers. The final round of storms finally moved offshore close to midnight after several hours of severe weather in the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and wires were downed near Kellers Rd and Mine Rd. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A moisture-laden system developed over the Gulf States and pushes up the spine of the Appalachians, bring a wintry mix of snow, sleet and freezing rain to central Pennsylvania from the evening of February 15 into the morning of February 16. The Lower Susquehanna Valley quickly went over to plain rain after a brief period of freezing rain, while the central mountains had a prolonged period of sleet and freezing rain with many locations receiving over 0.25 of ice accretion. North of I-80, there was 1-2 inches of snow and sleet followed by freezing rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A winter storm produced a quarter of an inch of ice accumulation, plus half an inch of sleet and an inch of snow to Warren County from February 15-16, 2021.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A southward moving cold front stalled across northern New Jersey and northeast Pennsylvania early on September 13. Warm and humid conditions were present south of the front. Combined with the instability, this disturbance caused a line of thunderstorms to move through the region during the evening hours of September 13. This line of storms became severe, with a number of reports of damaging wind along it. The line moved offshore and out of the region later that evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed on wires in Beaver Meadows. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A near record warm air mass was in place over the mid-Atlantic on June 30. Combined with fairly high humidity, moderate to strong instability built over the region. An approaching surface trough acted to trigger scattered thunderstorms over the area during the afternoon and evening hours. Shear was not very strong, which limited overall storm organization. However, some storms did become strong to severe and produced instances of damaging winds. Convective activity diminished during the later evening hours with the loss of daytime heating.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and wires were downed near Harrisburg School Rd. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very hot and humid air mass remained in place over the mid-Atlantic on June 9, following several days of unusually hot and humid conditions for the season. Similar to the previous day, afternoon thunderstorm development occurred in the mid-Atlantic mainly due to the influence of a weak cold front to the north and a weak surface trough. Like the previous day, storms were disorganized due to weak wind fields and a lack of forcing. However, the strong to extreme instability allowed some storms to briefly become severe with a threat for damaging winds, hail, and torrential rain. Convection gradually dissipated during the evening hours with the loss of daytime heating.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees and wires were downed in the area of where Lower Mountain Rd, Pineville Rd, and Street Rd intersect. A social media photo also showed damage to a chimney. The damage was likely caused by a downburst. Time estimated from radar and dispatch reports.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms developed ahead of an approaching cold front during the afternoon and evening of Wednesday, July 14.  Some of the storms produced damaging winds and numerous tornadoes.  Brief torrential rainfall was also observed with the stronger storm cells.  The areas that were hit hardest were in Buchanan, Delaware, Benton, Linn, and Jones counties in IA, where a total of 14 tornadoes occurred.  7 of the tornadoes had no visible damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Brief touchdown in a field with no visible damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A long-duration winter storm produced widespread snowfall across central Pennsylvania from January 31 to February 2, 2021. Although the snow began on January 31st, warning criteria was not met in any central Pennsylvania counties until February 1st or 2nd.  Widespread snowfall amounts of 10-15 inches were observed, with more than 20 inches of accumulation in portions of Schuylkill County. This was a Miller Type B storm, with the primarily low pushing up the Ohio Valley before a center-jump to the Mid-Atlantic coast was observed. Snow was the predominant precipitation type, although the Lower Susquehanna Valley had a several hour period of light wintry mix before the coastal low strengthened. The system then very slowly pulled east-northeastward along the southern New England coast and out to sea.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A winter storm produced 11 to 14 inches of snow across Montour County from January 31 to February 2, 2021.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As strengthening low pressure tracked through the Great Lakes on March 28, a strong cold front approached the mid-Atlantic coast. A narrow ribbon of modest instability developed ahead of the front. With strong wind fields in place and strong forcing from the cold front, a line of convection developed. The minimal instability caused this to be a low-topped convective line with little, though not zero, lightning. However, the strong forcing and wind fields caused the line to become a fairly prolific producer of straight line wind damage. A number of severe wind gusts were measured, with numerous reports of tree, utility, and some structural damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed onto wires on Reservoir Rd. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A long-duration winter storm produced widespread snowfall across central Pennsylvania from January 31 to February 2, 2021. Although the snow began on January 31st, warning criteria was not met in any central Pennsylvania counties until February 1st or 2nd.  Widespread snowfall amounts of 10-15 inches were observed, with more than 20 inches of accumulation in portions of Schuylkill County. This was a Miller Type B storm, with the primarily low pushing up the Ohio Valley before a center-jump to the Mid-Atlantic coast was observed. Snow was the predominant precipitation type, although the Lower Susquehanna Valley had a several hour period of light wintry mix before the coastal low strengthened. The system then very slowly pulled east-northeastward along the southern New England coast and out to sea.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A winter storm produced 8 to 10 inches of snow across Blair County from January 31 to February 2, 2021.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent surface low moved northeastward along a stationary front from northeast Indiana to far-southern Quebec during the wee hours through early afternoon of March 26th. Simultaneously, the trailing cold front swept eastward from near the Indiana/Ohio line to near Lake Champlain and northern Chesapeake Bay. A tight surface pressure gradient accompanying the low and rapid surface pressure rises behind the cold front contributed to damaging wind gusts in northwest Pennsylvania.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A long-duration winter storm produced widespread snowfall across central Pennsylvania from January 31 to February 2, 2021. Although the snow began on January 31st, warning criteria was not met in any central Pennsylvania counties until February 1st or 2nd.  Widespread snowfall amounts of 10-15 inches were observed, with more than 20 inches of accumulation in portions of Schuylkill County. This was a Miller Type B storm, with the primarily low pushing up the Ohio Valley before a center-jump to the Mid-Atlantic coast was observed. Snow was the predominant precipitation type, although the Lower Susquehanna Valley had a several hour period of light wintry mix before the coastal low strengthened. The system then very slowly pulled east-northeastward along the southern New England coast and out to sea.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A winter storm produced 10 to 16 inches of snow across Lebanon County from January 31 to February 2, 2021.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An isolated supercell developed behind a southward sagging frontal boundary.  With around 1000 J/kg MLCAPE and 40-45 knots of effective shear, a brief supercellular structure evolved. Even with hail size somewhat limited by available instability, substantial damage to total destruction of crops occurred due to the large quantity of wind-driven hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The wind-driven hail damage path continued out of Plymouth and Cherokee Counties into Woodbury County, where the continuous path ended around 2 miles east southeast of Pierson. The largest hail reported along the path was observed near Pierson with golf ball size hail at 1748 CST.  Half dollar size hail was reported at 1755 CST 3.5 miles north northwest of Correctionville. Crop damage is an estimate from insured losses. Information provided by the United States Department of Agriculture.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep western trough underwent lee-cyclogenesis across the southern Rockies with the low center tracking northeast across the southern Plains and into the midwest. Central and southern Iowa remained well within the deformation zone of the cyclone, allowing for the heaviest snow to fall in a band from southwest Iowa through central Iowa with a tight accumulation gradient across northern Iowa.  Forcing was particularly strong with the system, with lift within the dendritic growth zone exceeding -20 ubar/s for large portions of the state. Many areas saw snow rates exceed 1 inch per hour.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A band of mid-level frontogenesis set up near the Missouri River and eastward across northwest Iowa during the afternoon and evening of January 25, bringing a swath of moderate to briefly heavy snowfall. Dry air to the north resulted in a tight gradient to amounts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall totaled 7.0 inches 4 miles north northeast of Hornick and 5.7 inches in Sioux City.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong northwesterly jet streak digging through the central Rockies produced intense and deep cyclogenesis across Iowa on January 14 and 15. Initial precipitation swept through the area as rain, but a surge of cold air into the slowing cyclone wrapped snowfall back into northeast Nebraska as winds increased to 40 to 60 mph, resulting in periods of blizzard conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: As snow developed and began to accumulate during the evening on January 14, the increase in winds to a sustained 30 to 40 mph, with a few gusts as high as 51 mph at an Iowa Department of Transportation site at Alton and 44 mph near Maurice (SXK), resulted in widespread near white-out conditions. Shortly after snowfall began, a vehicle lost control and collided with another traveling in the opposite direction west of Alton, resulting in an indirect fatality to one driver and an indirect injury to the other. Snowfall totaled 3.0 inches at Sioux Center and 2.5 inches at Orange City.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system moved into the Midwest on the afternoon of January 30, 2021. Initially, precipitation began as rain as a layer of warm air was in place aloft. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall reports ranged from 2.8 inches in Clinton by the COOP observer to a public report of 3.0 inches in Charlotte.  The COOP observer also reported sleet and freezing rain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm affected the mid-Atlantic from January 31 to February 2, 2021. Low pressure tracking out of the Ohio Valley weakened as it moved slowly eastward on the 31st. Meanwhile, as that low weakened, secondary low pressure began to develop off the coast of the Carolinas and tracked northward, just off the mid-Atlantic coast. The low steadily intensified as it moved up the coast in a classic ���Miller B��� storm evolution. The result was a significant and unusually long duration winter storm. Overrunning precipitation associated with the initial low over the Ohio Valley impacted the region on the 31st. A cold antecedent air mass allowed most of this precipitation to fall as snow. This produced widespread snow accumulation, though the overrunning precipitation was mostly of the light to moderate variety. Some areas experienced a lull in precipitation on the overnight of the 31st as the secondary low began to develop and a dry slot overspread a large area. In addition, a surge of warmer air both at the surface and aloft caused precipitation to change to sleet or rain in some areas, especially locations farthest south and east such as the Delmarva peninsula and southern New Jersey. However, as the secondary low strengthened, heavy precipitation developed on February 1, with intense banding and areas of extreme snowfall rates of 2 to 4 inches per hour in northern New Jersey and portions of eastern Pennsylvania. Precipitation eventually turned back to snow all the way to the coastline as colder air was drawn in from the north. The secondary low pressure nearly stalled off the mid-Atlantic coast, causing snow to continue into February 2, although by then snowfall rates were much lighter and additional accumulation was limited. Areas where precipitation remained all snow and that experienced the heavy banding saw extreme snowfall totals, with isolated amounts of near 3 feet of snow and a fairly widespread swath of in excess of 2 feet. Snow flurries even continued into February 3 around the backside of the slow moving low���s large circulation, before it finally departed and brought an end to one of the region���s most notable snow events in years.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow began in the county on January 31 and continued into February 1 and 2, when the heaviest snow would fall.

Light lake effect snow developed over Lake Erie and pushed over Northwest Pennsylvania during the early evening hours of January 19. A shortwave trough entered the region and enhanced this lake effect snow late on the 19th into the 20th and a brief period of one inch per hour snowfall rates were reported in Erie County. Dry air quickly entered during the morning of January 20 and snow dissipated across the region. During this brief snow event, 8 inches of snow fell in a 12 hour period in North East Township in Erie County. Other snow totals include: 7.4 inches in Greenfield Township, 6.5 inches in Greene Township, 6.3 inches in Summit Township, and 5 inches in McKean. Lesser amounts were recorded elsewhere in Erie County. Impacts with this event were minimal.

A strong northwesterly jet streak digging through the central Rockies produced intense and deep cyclogenesis across Iowa on January 14 and 15. Initial precipitation swept through the area as rain, but a surge of cold air into the slowing cyclone wrapped snowfall back into northeast Nebraska as winds increased to 40 to 60 mph, resulting in periods of blizzard conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: As snow developed and began to accumulate during the evening on January 14, the increase in winds to a sustained 30 to 35 mph, with a few gusts as high as 41 mph at Cherokee (CKP), resulted in widespread near white-out conditions. Snowfall totaled 5.0 inches 4 miles north of Cleghorn and 3.0 inches at Cherokee.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm affected the mid-Atlantic from January 31 to February 2, 2021. Low pressure tracking out of the Ohio Valley weakened as it moved slowly eastward on the 31st. Meanwhile, as that low weakened, secondary low pressure began to develop off the coast of the Carolinas and tracked northward, just off the mid-Atlantic coast. The low steadily intensified as it moved up the coast in a classic ���Miller B��� storm evolution. The result was a significant and unusually long duration winter storm. Overrunning precipitation associated with the initial low over the Ohio Valley impacted the region on the 31st. A cold antecedent air mass allowed most of this precipitation to fall as snow. This produced widespread snow accumulation, though the overrunning precipitation was mostly of the light to moderate variety. Some areas experienced a lull in precipitation on the overnight of the 31st as the secondary low began to develop and a dry slot overspread a large area. In addition, a surge of warmer air both at the surface and aloft caused precipitation to change to sleet or rain in some areas, especially locations farthest south and east such as the Delmarva peninsula and southern New Jersey. However, as the secondary low strengthened, heavy precipitation developed on February 1, with intense banding and areas of extreme snowfall rates of 2 to 4 inches per hour in northern New Jersey and portions of eastern Pennsylvania. Precipitation eventually turned back to snow all the way to the coastline as colder air was drawn in from the north. The secondary low pressure nearly stalled off the mid-Atlantic coast, causing snow to continue into February 2, although by then snowfall rates were much lighter and additional accumulation was limited. Areas where precipitation remained all snow and that experienced the heavy banding saw extreme snowfall totals, with isolated amounts of near 3 feet of snow and a fairly widespread swath of in excess of 2 feet. Snow flurries even continued into February 3 around the backside of the slow moving low���s large circulation, before it finally departed and brought an end to one of the region���s most notable snow events in years.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow began in the county on January 31 and continued into February 1 and 2, when the heaviest snow would fall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: One person was killed in a single vehicle accident northwest of North Buena Vista (Clayton County) on January 16, 2021. Freezing drizzle coated the roads with a layer of ice causing the driver of a pickup truck to lose control on a curve, slide off the road and hit a rock bluff head-on. He was pronounced dead at the scene by authorities.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Weak low pressure passed offshore of the mid-Atlantic on February 18. Another weak, secondary wave of low pressure tracked along a similar path along a frontal zone trailing behind the primary low on the 19th. Strong high pressure over New England provided a cold air mass over the mid-Atlantic, leading to wintry precipitation as these areas of low pressure tracked offshore. The heaviest precipitation occurred with the primary wave on the 18th, with many areas seeing snow, some locally heavy, with a change to sleet and rain towards coastal areas. A narrow but intense band of precipitation provided a maximum in snowfall over portions of southeast Pennsylvania and central New Jersey. By the overnight of the 18th and into the 19th, precipitation became lighter, with a mix of light snow and light freezing rain or drizzle providing some additional accumulations and impacts. The system finally pulled away entirely by the late afternoon and evening of the 19th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow fell across the county, with an initial round of snow on the 18th, followed by a lull and some light freezing drizzle on the overnight of the 18th, then additional light snow on the 19th. Over the course of the event, a maximum storm total snowfall report of 5.8 inches was received from near Bossardsville. Several other 4 to 5 inch reports were received. The Mount Pocono (KMPO) ASOS recorded 0.04 inches of ice accretion from the freezing drizzle on the night of the 18th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms developed ahead of an approaching cold front during the afternoon and evening of Wednesday, July 14.  Some of the storms produced damaging winds and numerous tornadoes.  Brief torrential rainfall was also observed with the stronger storm cells.  The areas that were hit hardest were in Buchanan, Delaware, Benton, Linn, and Jones counties in IA, where a total of 14 tornadoes occurred.  7 of the tornadoes had no visible damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado began in Tama County and crossed into Benton County, just south of Dysart, around 6:08 pm CST. As the tornado entered Benton County, the max width was around 560 yards. This includes the main tornado and satellite vortices, which are supported by video evidence. The tornado caused damage to trees and farm outbuildings at a farmstead just over the county line. This damage was rated EF-1, with maximum winds around 100 mph. The tornado then followed an intermittent path to the east-northeast for about 4.5 miles through rural areas, before dissipating.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A fast moving wave of low pressure tracked northeastward off the Atlantic coast on February 7. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm affected the mid-Atlantic from January 31 to February 2, 2021. Low pressure tracking out of the Ohio Valley weakened as it moved slowly eastward on the 31st. Meanwhile, as that low weakened, secondary low pressure began to develop off the coast of the Carolinas and tracked northward, just off the mid-Atlantic coast. The low steadily intensified as it moved up the coast in a classic ���Miller B��� storm evolution. The result was a significant and unusually long duration winter storm. Overrunning precipitation associated with the initial low over the Ohio Valley impacted the region on the 31st. A cold antecedent air mass allowed most of this precipitation to fall as snow. This produced widespread snow accumulation, though the overrunning precipitation was mostly of the light to moderate variety. Some areas experienced a lull in precipitation on the overnight of the 31st as the secondary low began to develop and a dry slot overspread a large area. In addition, a surge of warmer air both at the surface and aloft caused precipitation to change to sleet or rain in some areas, especially locations farthest south and east such as the Delmarva peninsula and southern New Jersey. However, as the secondary low strengthened, heavy precipitation developed on February 1, with intense banding and areas of extreme snowfall rates of 2 to 4 inches per hour in northern New Jersey and portions of eastern Pennsylvania. Precipitation eventually turned back to snow all the way to the coastline as colder air was drawn in from the north. The secondary low pressure nearly stalled off the mid-Atlantic coast, causing snow to continue into February 2, although by then snowfall rates were much lighter and additional accumulation was limited. Areas where precipitation remained all snow and that experienced the heavy banding saw extreme snowfall totals, with isolated amounts of near 3 feet of snow and a fairly widespread swath of in excess of 2 feet. Snow flurries even continued into February 3 around the backside of the slow moving low���s large circulation, before it finally departed and brought an end to one of the region���s most notable snow events in years.

Lighter snow continued into February 2 before the storm finally departed. By the end of the event, a report was received from Coopersburg of 31.0 inches of snow. Numerous other reports of 24 to 30 inches of snow were received in the major winter storm. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm affected the mid-Atlantic from January 31 to February 2, 2021. Low pressure tracking out of the Ohio Valley weakened as it moved slowly eastward on the 31st. Meanwhile, as that low weakened, secondary low pressure began to develop off the coast of the Carolinas and tracked northward, just off the mid-Atlantic coast. The low steadily intensified as it moved up the coast in a classic ���Miller B��� storm evolution. The result was a significant and unusually long duration winter storm. Overrunning precipitation associated with the initial low over the Ohio Valley impacted the region on the 31st. A cold antecedent air mass allowed most of this precipitation to fall as snow. This produced widespread snow accumulation, though the overrunning precipitation was mostly of the light to moderate variety. Some areas experienced a lull in precipitation on the overnight of the 31st as the secondary low began to develop and a dry slot overspread a large area. In addition, a surge of warmer air both at the surface and aloft caused precipitation to change to sleet or rain in some areas, especially locations farthest south and east such as the Delmarva peninsula and southern New Jersey. However, as the secondary low strengthened, heavy precipitation developed on February 1, with intense banding and areas of extreme snowfall rates of 2 to 4 inches per hour in northern New Jersey and portions of eastern Pennsylvania. Precipitation eventually turned back to snow all the way to the coastline as colder air was drawn in from the north. The secondary low pressure nearly stalled off the mid-Atlantic coast, causing snow to continue into February 2, although by then snowfall rates were much lighter and additional accumulation was limited. Areas where precipitation remained all snow and that experienced the heavy banding saw extreme snowfall totals, with isolated amounts of near 3 feet of snow and a fairly widespread swath of in excess of 2 feet. Snow flurries even continued into February 3 around the backside of the slow moving low���s large circulation, before it finally departed and brought an end to one of the region���s most notable snow events in years.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow began across the county on January 31 and continued into the new month. Snow became heavy on February 1 as intense banding developed, with lighter snow continuing into February 2. By the end of the event, a trained spotter in Mount Pocono had amassed a storm total snowfall of 36.9 inches, which was also the highest storm total snow amount reported in this storm. A widespread 20 to 30 inches of snow fell throughout the county in one of the area's largest winter storms on record.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms developed ahead of an approaching cold front during the afternoon and evening of Wednesday, July 14.  Some of the storms produced damaging winds and numerous tornadoes.  Brief torrential rainfall was also observed with the stronger storm cells. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A fast moving arctic cold front brought dangerous conditions to portions of the area. Rain, mixed with freezing rain and sleet moved into eastern Iowa during the early morning, then as a cold front moved in from the west during the mid morning, the rain switched to snow. Strong winds and falling temperatures behind the front caused wet roads to quickly freeze.  Snow fell for several hours after the change over and became heavy at times, with widespread 2 to 6 inches of snowfall. Winds behind the front were 25 to 35 mph with gusts up to 45 mph during the afternoon and evening causing blowing snow in open areas. Whiteout conditions were seen in open areas, and some areas experienced periods of near blizzard conditions, especially across east central and  northeast Iowa. Significant drifting snow continued into Feb. 5.  Wind chills dropped to 5 below to 15 below zero late Thursday night and Friday morning along and north of I-80.||Key impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents, and road closures.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure passed over the Great Lakes and up the Saint Lawrence River valley from February 22 into February 23, 2021, pushing a warm front and cold front across central Pennsylvania. A narrow, north-south stripe of heavy snow (1-2 per hour) associated with the warm front passed over the Susquehanna Valley during the morning rush hour, and the heavy snowfall rates combined with the potential for a flash freeze prompted the issuance of snow squall warnings.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: SNOW SQUALL. A snow squall on the leading edge of a mesoscale band of heavy snow briefly dropped visibility to under one quarter mile in and produced flash-freeze conditions in eastern Cumberland County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm affected the mid-Atlantic from January 31 to February 2, 2021. Low pressure tracking out of the Ohio Valley weakened as it moved slowly eastward on the 31st. Meanwhile, as that low weakened, secondary low pressure began to develop off the coast of the Carolinas and tracked northward, just off the mid-Atlantic coast. The low steadily intensified as it moved up the coast in a classic ���Miller B��� storm evolution. The result was a significant and unusually long duration winter storm. Overrunning precipitation associated with the initial low over the Ohio Valley impacted the region on the 31st. A cold antecedent air mass allowed most of this precipitation to fall as snow. This produced widespread snow accumulation, though the overrunning precipitation was mostly of the light to moderate variety. Some areas experienced a lull in precipitation on the overnight of the 31st as the secondary low began to develop and a dry slot overspread a large area. In addition, a surge of warmer air both at the surface and aloft caused precipitation to change to sleet or rain in some areas, especially locations farthest south and east such as the Delmarva peninsula and southern New Jersey. However, as the secondary low strengthened, heavy precipitation developed on February 1, with intense banding and areas of extreme snowfall rates of 2 to 4 inches per hour in northern New Jersey and portions of eastern Pennsylvania. Precipitation eventually turned back to snow all the way to the coastline as colder air was drawn in from the north. The secondary low pressure nearly stalled off the mid-Atlantic coast, causing snow to continue into February 2, although by then snowfall rates were much lighter and additional accumulation was limited. Areas where precipitation remained all snow and that experienced the heavy banding saw extreme snowfall totals, with isolated amounts of near 3 feet of snow and a fairly widespread swath of in excess of 2 feet. Snow flurries even continued into February 3 around the backside of the slow moving low���s large circulation, before it finally departed and brought an end to one of the region���s most notable snow events in years.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow began on January 31. Precipitation continued into February 1. It decreased in intensity and also mixed with sleet for a time before changing back to snow later on February 1, when it also became heavy at times. Lighter snow continued into February 2. By the end of the event, a storm total snowfall of 15.0 inches was reported in Trappe. Numerous additional reports of 10 to 15 inches of snow were received.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved through the mid-Atlantic on February 22, with a developing wave of low pressure tracking northeast along the front just inland from the Atlantic coast. This fast moving system brought a period of steady precipitation to the region mainly during the morning and midday hours on the 22nd. A cold air mass was in place ahead of the system, causing precipitation to start as snow. Southerly winds ahead of the cold front brought warmer air into the region, causing a change from snow to rain in many areas. Despite it being a fairly atypical setup for wintry precipitation in the region, a brief but intense period of snow affected much of eastern Pennsylvania and northern New Jersey. Several inches of heavy, wet snow fell in just a few hours, causing considerable disruption on area roadways.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow fell across the county, which steadily changed to rain as warmer air moved in. In the northern portion of the county, a report of 3.3 inches of snow was received from Chestnut Hill. Further south, Philadelphia International Airport (KPHL) reported just 0.8 inches of snow. Both KPHL and Northeast Philadelphia Airport (KPNE) reported traces of freezing rain as snow changed to rain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The remnants of Hurricane Ida impacted the mid-Atlantic on September 1, 2021. As it moved northward, Ida began transitioning to a strong mid-latitude cyclone with pronounced frontal features, but with continued tropical moisture. On a regional level, the remnants of Ida became one of the most severe natural disasters in US history, due to a combination of several tornadoes, some of them strong, as well as catastrophic flooding over a large and densely populated area. The severe weather threat unfolded as the system's developing warm front lifted northward from the Delmarva region into Pennsylvania and New Jersey. South of the warm front, partial clearing and moderate to strong instability developed. Meanwhile, very strong shear and forcing, along with tropical moisture, were present within the warm sector. The result was widespread convection in the form of both supercell and quasi-linear thunderstorms. A number of storms became severe across the region, producing several tornadoes and other instances of wind damage. This continued an exceptionally active stretch of high end severe weather in the region, coming barely a month after the tornado outbreak of July 29.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado embedded within a squall line developed several miles |southeast of the storm which produced a tornado in Buckingham |Township. Tornadic damage was first observed in the vicinity of |Stoneybrook Rd at Eagle Rd, near Jericho Creek. The tornado |tracked northeastward from there. It passed over the Jericho |National Golf Club, and sporadic tree damage mainly consisting of |uproots and large limbs snapped was observed in a path throughout |the golf course. It then moved over the adjacent Brownsburg Park, |where additional tree damage was observed and several soccer goals|were observed flipped in various directions. The tornado then |began to approach the Delaware River. Some minor tree damage was |observed along River Rd. However, the tornado appeared to lift |just slightly before reaching the Delaware River, with no apparent|damage on Pebbletown Rd just prior to the river. Throughout its |path, the tree damage produced by this tornado was fairly |sporadic, and it may have been discontinuous. Noticeable wind |damage was also observed for at least a mile east of the tornado |track, especially near its endpoint close to the Delaware River. |This is believed to be straight line wind damage, which is |corroborated by radar data, occurring around the rear flank |downdraft region of the tornadic circulation. However, the exact |length and width of the tornadic circulation is somewhat uncertain|due to the surrounding areas of straight line wind damage.
