EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough dropped out of the Canadian Rockies and across the upper midwest. Storms developed along a surface boundary in the afternoon, resulting in a few hail reports and a strong wind gust. In addition to the moderate CAPE , the backed wind profile supported some rotation within storms. While no tornadoes occurred there was a funnel cloud reported north of the Des Moines metro.  Later that night the deep warm cloud layer and high precipitable water values made for efficient rain producers. As storms continued overnight along a stationary boundary locally heavy rain resulted in flash flooding in central Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 24 hour rain total of 4.28 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As deep layer moisture increased ahead of an approaching cold front on July 1, 2022, low level convergence on the leading edge of moisture advection coincided with lift associated with the right entrance region of a 95KT upper jet. The downburst potential was enhanced by a layer of dry air in the environment above 750 hPa, which resulted in DCAPE values of 1200-1300 J/kg through the day and into the evening hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of thunderstorms developed across eastern Montana and the western Dakotas during the morning hours. These storms organized and turned southeastward, feeding on rich inflow of post-frontal air with up to 3000 J/kg of MLCAPE and over 1000 J/kg of DCAPE. Along with strong storm-relative shear, parameters favored development of a strong cold pool and balanced mesocyclone, which spread southeast with the cluster and developed a strong and long-duration severe wind event which traversed South Dakota, southwest Minnesota, extreme northeast Nebraska, and northwest Iowa during the afternoon and early evening. The storm was classified as a derecho, and featured numerous wind gusts from 70 to 100 mph and considerable damage to trees, crops, powerlines, and structures along its path.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were downed just west of Royal by thunderstorm wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An amplified and vigorous upper level pattern pushed several weak disturbances northeast across the region during the overnight and early morning of May 30th. With ample elevated instability on the order of 2000-2500 J/kg available and effective shear of 35 to 45 knots, storms became severe across south central South Dakota and north central Nebraska and organized into a large scale QLCS as it moved east and northeast into Minnesota and Iowa late night. Several QLCS tornadoes developed from the Sioux Falls area eastward. Widespread winds of 60 to 90 mph caused scattered tree damage, with isolated pockets of more significant structural damage. Presidential Disaster Declarations were granted to Lyon, Rock, and Nobles Counties in Minnesota for damages to public infrastructure.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds damaged several outbuildings and downed several trees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As deep layer moisture increased ahead of an approaching cold front on July 1, 2022, low level convergence on the leading edge of moisture advection coincided with lift associated with the right entrance region of a 95KT upper jet. The result was multiple clusters of thunderstorms moving across the southern half of central PA through the afternoon, several of which produced isolated areas of straight line wind damage. Another line of convection developed closer to the cold front during the evening in NW Pennsylvania and moved southeastward, producing isolated straight line wind damage until about 1:00 AM EDT on July 2. The downburst potential was enhanced by a layer of dry air in the environment above 750 hPa, which resulted in DCAPE values of 1200-1300 J/kg through the day and into the evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing winds estimated near 60 mph snapped a tree, with a large limb landing on the roof of a house in the 2600 block of Stoverstown Road near Spring Grove.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An amplified and vigorous upper level pattern pushed several weak disturbances northeast across the region during the overnight and early morning of May 30th. With ample elevated instability on the order of 2000-2500 J/kg available and effective shear of 35 to 45 knots, storms became severe across south central South Dakota and north central Nebraska and organized into a large scale QLCS as it moved east and northeast into Minnesota and Iowa late night. Several QLCS tornadoes developed from the Sioux Falls area eastward. Widespread winds of 60 to 90 mph caused scattered tree damage, with isolated pockets of more significant structural damage. Presidential Disaster Declarations were granted to Lyon, Rock, and Nobles Counties in Minnesota for damages to public infrastructure.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm wind gust of 60 mph was measured by the Automated Surface Observing System site KSPW 4 miles west-northwest of Spencer.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A volatile environment featured a warm front from parts of east central South Dakota into western Minnesota, with a dryline extending to the southwest into Nebraska. With a very strong wave moving northeast through Nebraska into a highly unstable and highly sheared environment, scattered storms initiated and quickly grew upscale to a broad linear structure with damaging winds. With crop development well behind schedule and many fields yet to be planted, there was ample dirt available to be lofted into the leading edge of the storms, which took on the characteristics of a haboob reducing visibility to near zero at the onset of high winds.||A broad swath of winds from 70 to 100 mph devastated much of southeast South Dakota, and portions of southwest Minnesota, northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, causing extensive tree and structural damage and scores of injuries. The highest observed wind gust was 107 mph near Tripp, SD. In addition, vehicles and high profile vehicles were blown off several roads, shutting down traffic on Interstates 29 and 90. Two (direct) fatalities occurred in vehicles impacted by debris as the storms moved into the Sioux Falls area. Power was disrupted in a widespread area, with estimates of over 45,000 customers impacted at one time. Many schools were closed due to damage and power issues. The South Dakota Governor requested and was granted a Presidential Disaster Declaration for damage to public infrastructure at an estimated cost of 6.7 million dollars across 20 counties and two reservations. Private losses were a much higher toll, and just one of the impacted counties (McCook) estimated at least 150 to 175 million dollars in damage. Presidential Disaster Declarations were also granted in Dixon County, Nebraska and Lincoln County, Minnesota.||Following the afternoon line of storms, a secondary band of storms developed near the core of the upper level jet across eastern Nebraska in the early evening hours. These storms also quickly become severe, with a mix of large hail, damaging wind, and even an isolated tornado near Sioux City. This cluster of storms moved through far southeast South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A video showed a brief tornado crossing Interstate 29 between Sergeant Bluff and Port Neal. The tornado caused no damage from which the NWS could assign an EF-scale rating.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong storms that produced damaging winds developed the evening of June 22, 2022. A broken line of showers and storms developed between Cleveland and Pittsburgh just before 3pm and continue to advances southeast along the axis of a trough entering from the north. Dry conditions under ridging hours ahead of the showers and storms helped prime the environment. Mean level CAPE before convective was between 3000-3500J/kg, and steep lapse rates near the surface (7.5 to 8.0C/km) help with strong damaging updrafts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Fire and Rescue reports trees down on Graham and Hilltop Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of thunderstorms focused near Cleveland became organized (into a squall line) the evening of June 1st and unleashed strong damaging wind north and west of Pittsburgh. Storms lost their intensity as they approached Pittsburgh and a gust front jetted out ahead of the line of convection, approaching an area that lacked robust instability.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A new mesoscale convective system (MCS) developed from the outflow of a previously mature MCS in southern Wisconsin before venturing southeast into the Ohio River Valley the evening of June 13th. Strong winds from Indiana to eastern Ohio were measured and observed; the Fort Wayne International Airport in the state of Indiana measured a wind gust of 98mph. ||The county that was hit the hardest was Tuscarawas, as a rear inflow jet advances from the northwest. Drones, a damage survey team, and aerial satellite data (Sentinel 2) showed numerous swaths of tree damage in central Tuscarawas County. Isolated areas  experienced wind damage equivalent to an EF2 tornado (wind gusts up to 120mph).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Cove Road blocked due to downed tree landing on road and power lines. Over 700 people without power across the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system brought much needed rainfall to eastern Iowa the morning of November 4th through the 5th. This also brought two rounds of severe weather to eastern Iowa. The morning of November 4th, a few storms cells intensified quickly and produced sporadic reports of hail that was penny to ping pong ball sized. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of storms moved across northeast Iowa during the evening of July 23rd. These storms produced an EF1 tornado west of Waukon (Allamakee County) that damaged a farm and trees. Strong thunderstorm winds caused extensive damage to several buildings at the community college in Calmar (Winneshiek County) and flipped over a couple vehicles. The public school athletic fields in Calmar were also heavily damaged. The press box was blown off the high school football stands, metal light poles were downed at the softball field, and metal bleachers were thrown over a fence and onto the field. In Waukon, the roofs were damaged on numerous buildings and several trees and power lines were blown down. The Governor of Iowa issued a disaster proclamation for Allamakee, Clayton and Winneshiek Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An estimated 60 mph wind gust occurred west of Waukon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved across Iowa overnight from the 14th to 15th of June. The week had been steamy with near record highs and high humidity, making for a highly unstable airmass with CAPE over 3000 J/kg. Storms initiated along the front in central Iowa later on June 14th, resulting in a number of hail and wind damage reports. While storms dropped below severe limits shortly after midnight, heavy rain continued as thunderstorms trained along the nearly stationary front. This resulted in localized areas received two to four plus inches of rain that flooded a few area roadways.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees down and roof damage with strong winds. Time estimated via radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system brought much needed rainfall to eastern Iowa the morning of November 4th through the 5th. This also brought two rounds of severe weather to eastern Iowa. During the morning hours of the 5th, a cold front moved eastward across the area couple with a low level jet led to a rapidly strengthening line of thunderstorms across far eastern Iowa that produced strong winds. The strongest winds along this line occurred in Scott and Muscatine County where damaging winds were reported. Heavy rain also fell with this storm system with 48 hour rainfall totals of 1 to 4 inches across eastern Iowa with the heaviest rains being reported along a Ottumwa to Dubuque line.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS Employee reported a tree down near their residence. The time of the event was estimated using radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A few rounds of thunderstorms on July 24th and 25th preceded a cold frontal passage.  High levels of instability, ample shear, and pre-frontal disturbances provided thunderstorm clusters producing widespread damaging wind gusts.  Many instances of tree and power line damage were noted, along with isolated instances of structural damage.  One of those instances of structural damage, a tree falling on to two trailers in Venango County, unfortunately led to the death of a 28 year old woman.  Flash flooding of urbanized areas of Allegheny County also occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees were reported down on Beham Ridge Road in West Findley Township.

A line of storms moved across northeast Iowa during the evening of July 23rd. These storms produced an EF1 tornado west of Waukon (Allamakee County) that damaged a farm and trees. Strong thunderstorm winds caused extensive damage to several buildings at the community college in Calmar (Winneshiek County) and flipped over a couple vehicles. The public school athletic fields in Calmar were also heavily damaged. The press box was blown off the high school football stands, metal light poles were downed at the softball field, and metal bleachers were thrown over a fence and onto the field. In Waukon, the roofs were damaged on numerous buildings and several trees and power lines were blown down. The Governor of Iowa issued a disaster proclamation for Allamakee, Clayton and Winneshiek Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An estimated 60 mph wind gust occurred in Waukon. The roof was blown off a business, a home lost part of its roof and several other businesses sustained some roof damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low for a few days July 7th and 8th. While the parameter space was not conducive to strong convection, the steep lapse rates, low LCLs, and sufficient 0-3 km CAPE resulted in a favorable environment for funnel cloud development both days. Several funnel clouds were reported across central and northern Iowa, along with two tornadoes documented under developing storms during the afternoon of July 7th.  These spin-ups remained in open areas with little damage. Storms were also efficient rain producers, with a pocket of 3 to 5 inches in Hardin and Grundy counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Funnel cloud spotted east of Estherville. Report from social media.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Another shortwave moved across Iowa in early June, this one resulting in severe storms across southwest Iowa. Modest CAPE around 1000 J/kg was accompanied by deep layer shear that helped to organize storms and support rotating updrafts capable of large hail and damaging winds. By evening storms across southwest Iowa were producing up to golf ball sized hail and winds damaged several trees and outbuildings.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees, sheds, and power lines reported down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved across Iowa overnight from the 14th to 15th of June. The week had been steamy with near record highs and high humidity, making for a highly unstable airmass with CAPE over 3000 J/kg. Storms initiated along the front in central Iowa later on June 14th, resulting in a number of hail and wind damage reports. While storms dropped below severe limits shortly after midnight, heavy rain continued as thunderstorms trained along the nearly stationary front. This resulted in localized areas received two to four plus inches of rain that flooded a few area roadways.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level trough produced widespread showers and thunderstorms across the Midwest. Meanwhile, isolated storms developed behind the primary area of convection while instability remained high and shear was still in place to help organize storms. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough and an associated surface cold front tracked eastward from the Midwest and across the Upper Ohio Valley on November 18th. Steep low level lapse rates, moisture in the dendritic growth region, strong vorticity-supported ascent, and some minimal surface-based CAPE, resulted in numerous snow showers.  One cluster produced snow squall conditions as it tracked across southwest Pennsylvania between noon and 5 PM, with quick accumulations of one to two inches and visibilities of one-quarter mile or less. Thankfully, no major traffic incidents were reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow squall. At the Connellsville AWOS site, visibility dropped to one-quarter mile in heavy snow and wind gusted to 25 MPH.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave pushed across the Midwest, resulting a a period of severe storms. the leading moisture axis and warm front were confined main to Minnesota in the afternoon, though a few stronger storms skimmed northern Iowa with a hail report in Winnebago county. The cold front passed across Iowa later in the evening from western to northern Iowa. Modest CAPE was in place but with strong deep layer shear over 40 kts and drier low levels noted in model soundings, gusty winds were the primary hazard with this second round of thunderstorms. Winds gusted over 60 mph with a few reports of damage to trees and outbuildings.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter estimated 60 mph gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of thunderstorms developed across eastern Montana and the western Dakotas during the morning hours. These storms organized and turned southeastward, feeding on rich inflow of post-frontal air with up to 3000 J/kg of MLCAPE and over 1000 J/kg of DCAPE. Along with strong storm-relative shear, parameters favored development of a strong cold pool and balanced mesocyclone, which spread southeast with the cluster and developed a strong and long-duration severe wind event which traversed South Dakota, southwest Minnesota, extreme northeast Nebraska, and northwest Iowa during the afternoon and early evening. The storm was classified as a derecho, and featured numerous wind gusts from 70 to 100 mph and considerable damage to trees, crops, powerlines, and structures along its path.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms winds snapped a 150 foot tree in Sutherland - at the time the largest tree in O'Brien County.  Limbs which fell on powerlines resulted in up to 5 hours without power.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A long-duration, multi-faceted winter storm hit northwestern Pennsylvania just before Christmas 2022 with extreme cold, strong winds, accumulating snow and extensive blowing and drifting of the snow that fell. An Arctic cold front swept east across northwestern Pennsylvania during the early morning hours of December 23rd. Low pressure along this front tracked over Lake Erie early in the morning on December 23rd and rapidly intensified through the day while slowly lifting northeast across Ontario. With the frontal passage rain changed to snow with temperatures dropping from the upper 30s and lower 40s to sub-zero in about 8 hours. The snow was generally light to moderate, but a brief period of heavier snow with rates of around one inch per hour lifted through during the morning hours December 23rd. The period of snow and rapidly falling temperatures led to a flash freeze and icy conditions on area roadways. While the falling snow became lighter through the afternoon hours of December 23rd, winds began increasing during the morning and gusted over 40 MPH through the day. Peak gusts of up to 55 MPH were measured near the Lake Erie shoreline. Peak gusts across the rest of northwestern Pennsylvania were generally 40-50 MPH. Wind gusts very gradually subsided into December 24th, though gusts didn���t drop below 30mph until that evening. This led to a prolonged period of widespread blowing and drifting snow beginning during the morning December 23rd and continuing through the afternoon and evening, with some patchy blowing and drifting snow continuing overnight and all the way through Christmas Eve. In parts of northwestern Pennsylvania the blowing and drifting snow was extensive enough to lead to blizzard conditions on December 23rd. This storm caused a number of impacts across the area. The greatest impact was to travel due to the flash freeze and extensive blowing and drifting snow, to go along with low visibility. Numerous minor accidents, slide-offs and disabled vehicles were reported throughout the area on December 23rd and 24th. Wind chills dipped to -25 to -40 across all of northwestern Pennsylvania on December 23rd. A number of burst pipes were reported across northwestern Pennsylvania due to this cold, with temperatures remaining in the single digits until Christmas morning. Erie International Airport recorded 3.0��� of snow with this storm, with amounts as high as 8.0��� measured by a trained spotter in Greenfield Township.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills plunged below 0 around 8 AM December 23rd and did not warm above 0 until midday December 26th. A minimum wind chill of -30 degrees was reported at 2:51 PM December 23rd at Erie International Airport. Warming centers were opened in Erie and Mill Village in response to these conditions. A number of burst pipes were reported across Northwest Pennsylvania due to this cold, with temperatures remaining in the single digits until Christmas morning.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A long-duration, multi-faceted winter storm hit northwestern Pennsylvania just before Christmas 2022 with extreme cold, strong winds, accumulating snow and extensive blowing and drifting of the snow that fell. An Arctic cold front swept east across northwestern Pennsylvania during the early morning hours of December 23rd. Low pressure along this front tracked over Lake Erie early in the morning on December 23rd and rapidly intensified through the day while slowly lifting northeast across Ontario. With the frontal passage rain changed to snow with temperatures dropping from the upper 30s and lower 40s to sub-zero in about 8 hours. The snow was generally light to moderate, but a brief period of heavier snow with rates of around one inch per hour lifted through during the morning hours December 23rd. The period of snow and rapidly falling temperatures led to a flash freeze and icy conditions on area roadways. While the falling snow became lighter through the afternoon hours of December 23rd, winds began increasing during the morning and gusted over 40 MPH through the day. Peak gusts of up to 55 MPH were measured near the Lake Erie shoreline. Peak gusts across the rest of northwestern Pennsylvania were generally 40-50 MPH. Wind gusts very gradually subsided into December 24th, though gusts didn���t drop below 30mph until that evening. This led to a prolonged period of widespread blowing and drifting snow beginning during the morning December 23rd and continuing through the afternoon and evening, with some patchy blowing and drifting snow continuing overnight and all the way through Christmas Eve. In parts of northwestern Pennsylvania the blowing and drifting snow was extensive enough to lead to blizzard conditions on December 23rd. This storm caused a number of impacts across the area. The greatest impact was to travel due to the flash freeze and extensive blowing and drifting snow, to go along with low visibility. Numerous minor accidents, slide-offs and disabled vehicles were reported throughout the area on December 23rd and 24th. Wind chills dipped to -25 to -40 across all of northwestern Pennsylvania on December 23rd. A number of burst pipes were reported across northwestern Pennsylvania due to this cold, with temperatures remaining in the single digits until Christmas morning. Erie International Airport recorded 3.0��� of snow with this storm, with amounts as high as 8.0��� measured by a trained spotter in Greenfield Township.

A minimum wind chill of -32 degrees was reported at 5:01 PM at Meadville Airport. Weather stations reported minimum wind chills of -32 in Richmond Township and -31 outside of Saegertown. A number of burst pipes were reported across Northwest Pennsylvania due to this cold, with temperatures remaining in the single digits until Christmas morning.

With ample elevated instability on the order of 2000-2500 J/kg available and effective shear of 35 to 45 knots, storms became severe across south central South Dakota and north central Nebraska and organized into a large scale QLCS as it moved east and northeast into Minnesota and Iowa late night. Several QLCS tornadoes developed from the Sioux Falls area eastward. Widespread winds of 60 to 90 mph caused scattered tree damage, with isolated pockets of more significant structural damage. Presidential Disaster Declarations were granted to Lyon, Rock, and Nobles Counties in Minnesota for damages to public infrastructure.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts brought down numerous large tree limbs, with several trees snapped or uprooted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of thunderstorms developed across eastern Montana and the western Dakotas during the morning hours. These storms organized and turned southeastward, feeding on rich inflow of post-frontal air with up to 3000 J/kg of MLCAPE and over 1000 J/kg of DCAPE. The storm was classified as a derecho, and featured numerous wind gusts from 70 to 100 mph and considerable damage to trees, crops, powerlines, and structures along its path.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees and power lines downed by thunderstorm winds in George.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level trough produced widespread showers and thunderstorms across the Midwest. A few non sever thunderstorms developed along the front, one of which produced a brief funnel cloud in northeast Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 24 hour rain total of 4 inches.

Convection lasted much of the evening and overnight across southern Iowa with several of the multicell storms producing severe hail. In addition, storms produced pockets of heavy rain with area receiving three to five inches of rain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong, occluding surface low crossed the Great Lakes on November 27th. After morning rain, instability in the form of around 500 J/kg of mean-layer CAPE was able to develop in the Middle Ohio Valley and advect northeast into northern West Virginia and southwest Pennsylvania.  A strongly sheared environment was also present. Strong low-level flow helped to support a damaging-wind threat, while cold temperatures aloft and favorable deep-layer shear also supported large hail, which is unusual for late November.  In fact, severe conditions were locally quite signficant, with one report of an 87 MPH gust in a mesovortex, as well as hail reaching two inches in diameter.  Many reports of downed trees and power lines were received, with some generally minor structural damage as well.  In Perry Township, estimates were that up to 400 vehicles were damaged by hail, with an estimated 1.2 million dollars worth of damage. A similar amount of car damage also likely occurred in Westmoreland County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Lake effect rain impacted Erie County beginning early in the morning of September 25th as a seasonally cold airmass moved southeast across the Great Lakes region. Lake effect rain continued on and off through the 25th and 26th before a more concentrated rain band focused on the western portion of Erie County during the morning and midday hours of September 27th. This additional rain resulted in minor areal flooding across the western portion of the county, with several road closures coincident with overflowing creeks and streams. Total rainfall over a three day period from September 25th through September 27th ranged from 3 to 6 inches over western Erie County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: County dispatch reported the eastbound portion of Pennsylvania State Route 5 was closed just east of Pennsylvania State Route 215 in North Springfield due to flooding of Crooked Creek. The eastbound portion of the roadway was damaged due to the flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved across Iowa, allowing for a longer duration rainfall event  with central and southeast Iowa picking up a widespread two to three inches with a few location seeing up to four inches of rain. While storms were initially discrete with a few stronger cores, they remained below severe limits and quickly grew into a stratiform regime with little lightning. While this rain helped to ease drought conditions in parts of the state, the precipitation deficit for the year remained high.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 24 hour rain total of 2.14 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong, occluding surface low crossed the Great Lakes on November 27th. After morning rain, instability in the form of around 500 J/kg of mean-layer CAPE was able to develop in the Middle Ohio Valley and advect northeast into northern West Virginia and southwest Pennsylvania.  A strongly sheared environment was also present. Strong low-level flow helped to support a damaging-wind threat, while cold temperatures aloft and favorable deep-layer shear also supported large hail, which is unusual for late November.  In fact, severe conditions were locally quite signficant, with one report of an 87 MPH gust in a mesovortex, as well as hail reaching two inches in diameter.  Many reports of downed trees and power lines were received, with some generally minor structural damage as well.  In Perry Township, estimates were that up to 400 vehicles were damaged by hail, with an estimated 1.2 million dollars worth of damage. A similar amount of car damage also likely occurred in Westmoreland County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Southwest flow during the late morning and early afternoon hours of September 21st advected warm, high dewpoint air into the region that was unusual for late September.  By late afternoon, a pre-frontal trough entered the area.   Thunderstorms crossing Lake Erie and arriving in western Pennsylvania during the late afternoon were hindered by warm air aloft, and thus were not able to achieve the overall coverage and intensity that had been anticipated.  Nevertheless, renewed convection along a cold front provided sufficient lift to create more widespread storms after midnight on the 22nd, and a few instances of wind damage resulted.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were reported down near Hillsville Road.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Portions of Lucas county remained in severe drought for all of September. Abnormally low rainfall continues to produce widespread drought conditions late into the growing season. Impacts are likely to crop yields across the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough supplied enough moisture and weak lift to sustain non sever convection through much of the morning of September 17th. By evening a secondary lobe of low pressure lifted into Iowa, enhancing convective development. MLCAPE over 2000 J/kg, curve hodographs, and steep mid level lapse rates supported large hail development. Convection lasted much of the evening and overnight across southern Iowa with several of the multicell storms producing severe hail. In addition, storms produced pockets of heavy rain with area receiving three to five inches of rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Day total up to 10 pm. Heaviest rain fell between 730 pm and 9 pm.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak area of low pressure pushed up the Ohio Valley during the afternoon and evening of November 15, 2022. This system pushed wet snow into central Pennsylvania, with light rain in the Lower Susquehanna Valley. A quick 3 to 5 inches of snow accumulated from the Laurel Highlands northeastward across the Ridge and Valley region. Although it was only an Advisory-level event, it was the first accumulating snowfall of the year and there were numerous traffic accidents and road closures.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A period of moderate snow led to slick roads and a two-vehicle accident with one fatality and two injuries (one serious) on the 3000 block of Route 96 (Hyndman Road) near Hyndman. The road was closed for over three hours, with traffic being rerouted around the scene of the accident.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms developed across portions of eastern Iowa, northwest Illinois, and far northeast Missouri on the evening of September 18, 2022. Storms initially developed near the Iowa/Missouri border, with one storm near Bloomfield IA producing a well defined wall cloud before weakening. Storms developed and increased in strength just east of the Cedar Rapids and Iowa City metros as they slowly tracked east around the Interstate 80 corridor. Several large hail reports were received around Durant to south of Tipton, with the largest report being 2.5 inches. Storms also produced small hail and wind damage in the Quad Cities before spreading southeast into Henry County IL. Additional storms developed along the Iowa/Missouri/Illinois tri-state area, with several tornado warnings issued. Damage was reported in southern Hancock County near Tioga, and continued south into Adams County, although no tornadoes were confirmed.

A quick 3 to 5 inches of snow accumulated from the Laurel Highlands northeastward across the Ridge and Valley region. Although it was only an Advisory-level event, it was the first accumulating snowfall of the year and there were numerous traffic accidents and road closures.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A period of moderate snow led to slick roads, leading to a fatal vehicle accident on the southbound lanes of I-81 in Lebanon County. The southbound lanes were closed for over 3 hours so that the state police could perform an accident reconstruction.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front plowed into an environment with roughly 1500 J/kg MLCAPE but weak shear, which resulted in numerous thunderstorms with brief intense updrafts. The strongest storms produced isolated damaging wind gusts and hail up to golf ball size. By evening, a stronger low-level flow ahead of the front resulted in a slightly stronger storm with hail up to 2.5 inches in diameter across northwest Iowa.

A strong, occluding surface low crossed the Great Lakes on November 27th. After morning rain, instability in the form of around 500 J/kg of mean-layer CAPE was able to develop in the Middle Ohio Valley and advect northeast into northern West Virginia and southwest Pennsylvania.  A strongly sheared environment was also present. Strong low-level flow helped to support a damaging-wind threat, while cold temperatures aloft and favorable deep-layer shear also supported large hail, which is unusual for late November.  In fact, severe conditions were locally quite signficant, with one report of an 87 MPH gust in a mesovortex, as well as hail reaching two inches in diameter.  Many reports of downed trees and power lines were received, with some generally minor structural damage as well.  In Perry Township, estimates were that up to 400 vehicles were damaged by hail, with an estimated 1.2 million dollars worth of damage. A similar amount of car damage also likely occurred in Westmoreland County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A roof was partially blown off of a house.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough supplied enough moisture and weak lift to sustain non sever convection through much of the morning of September 17th. By evening a secondary lobe of low pressure lifted into Iowa, enhancing convective development. MLCAPE over 2000 J/kg, curve hodographs, and steep mid level lapse rates supported large hail development. Convection lasted much of the evening and overnight across southern Iowa with several of the multicell storms producing severe hail. In addition, storms produced pockets of heavy rain with area receiving three to five inches of rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 24 hour rain total of 3.30 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms developed across portions of eastern Iowa, northwest Illinois, and far northeast Missouri on the evening of September 18, 2022. Storms initially developed near the Iowa/Missouri border, with one storm near Bloomfield IA producing a well defined wall cloud before weakening. Storms developed and increased in strength just east of the Cedar Rapids and Iowa City metros as they slowly tracked east around the Interstate 80 corridor. Several large hail reports were received around Durant to south of Tipton, with the largest report being 2.5 inches. Storms also produced small hail and wind damage in the Quad Cities before spreading southeast into Henry County IL. Additional storms developed along the Iowa/Missouri/Illinois tri-state area, with several tornado warnings issued. Damage was reported in southern Hancock County near Tioga, and continued south into Adams County, although no tornadoes were confirmed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report through social media, estimating quarter sized hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A volatile environment featured a warm front from parts of east central South Dakota into western Minnesota, with a dryline extending to the southwest into Nebraska. With a very strong wave moving northeast through Nebraska into a highly unstable and highly sheared environment, scattered storms initiated and quickly grew upscale to a broad linear structure with damaging winds. With crop development well behind schedule and many fields yet to be planted, there was ample dirt available to be lofted into the leading edge of the storms, which took on the characteristics of a haboob reducing visibility to near zero at the onset of high winds.||A broad swath of winds from 70 to 100 mph devastated much of southeast South Dakota, and portions of southwest Minnesota, northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, causing extensive tree and structural damage and scores of injuries. The highest observed wind gust was 107 mph near Tripp, SD. In addition, vehicles and high profile vehicles were blown off several roads, shutting down traffic on Interstates 29 and 90. Two (direct) fatalities occurred in vehicles impacted by debris as the storms moved into the Sioux Falls area. Power was disrupted in a widespread area, with estimates of over 45,000 customers impacted at one time. Many schools were closed due to damage and power issues. The South Dakota Governor requested and was granted a Presidential Disaster Declaration for damage to public infrastructure at an estimated cost of 6.7 million dollars across 20 counties and two reservations. Private losses were a much higher toll, and just one of the impacted counties (McCook) estimated at least 150 to 175 million dollars in damage. Presidential Disaster Declarations were also granted in Dixon County, Nebraska and Lincoln County, Minnesota.||Following the afternoon line of storms, a secondary band of storms developed near the core of the upper level jet across eastern Nebraska in the early evening hours. These storms also quickly become severe, with a mix of large hail, damaging wind, and even an isolated tornado near Sioux City. This cluster of storms moved through far southeast South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Three inch branches were downed by thunderstorm winds.

After morning rain, instability in the form of around 500 J/kg of mean-layer CAPE was able to develop in the Middle Ohio Valley and advect northeast into northern West Virginia and southwest Pennsylvania.  A strongly sheared environment was also present. Strong low-level flow helped to support a damaging-wind threat, while cold temperatures aloft and favorable deep-layer shear also supported large hail, which is unusual for late November.  In fact, severe conditions were locally quite signficant, with one report of an 87 MPH gust in a mesovortex, as well as hail reaching two inches in diameter.  Many reports of downed trees and power lines were received, with some generally minor structural damage as well.  In Perry Township, estimates were that up to 400 vehicles were damaged by hail, with an estimated 1.2 million dollars worth of damage. A similar amount of car damage also likely occurred in Westmoreland County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were reported to be blown down along Route 30.

The second closure was Route 770 (Minard Run Road), which was closed due to a disabled tractor trailer at the top of a hill in Bradford Township.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough supplied enough moisture and weak lift to sustain non sever convection through much of the morning of September 17th. By evening a secondary lobe of low pressure lifted into Iowa, enhancing convective development. MLCAPE over 2000 J/kg, curve hodographs, and steep mid level lapse rates supported large hail development. Convection lasted much of the evening and overnight across southern Iowa with several of the multicell storms producing severe hail. In addition, storms produced pockets of heavy rain with area receiving three to five inches of rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Penny and nickel sized hail with some up to quarter sized mixed in.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A reinforcing shot of unseasonably cold air led to a broken line of snow squalls that pushed from west to east across central Pennsylvania during the afternoon of November 18, 2022. These squalls reduced visibility to a quarter mile or less and were accompanied by gusty winds. Surface temperatures were just above freezing for many locations at the onset of the squalls, and flash-freezing was a concern.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: SNOW SQUALL. A broken line of snow squalls accompanied by gusty winds produced brief whiteout conditions as it crossed Sullivan County during that late afternoon of November 18, 2022. This led to a three-vehicle accident on US Route 220 that closed the road in both directions (for over 2 hours) between PA Route 87 and Shinerville Road in Cherry Township. There was one injury reported. The road closure was prolonged by a tractor tralier that ignored the detour and got stuck.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unusually long-lasting daylight dense fog event developed across most of eastern Pennsylvania on December 31st, 2022. The event resulted due to much warmer moist air moving northward in association with a warm front, crossing over areas where the ground remained frozen following the severe cold snap a week earlier. The fog started developing across southeastern portions of the area, then spread northwestward, enveloping most of the area at various points during the morning, afternoon and evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several hours of dense fog was observed at Northeast Philadelphia Airport and Doylestown Airport.

On March 5, 2022 a total of 15 tornadoes occurred across the state of Iowa as a warm front lifted across the area. Supercells initially developed across southwest Iowa in the vicinity of the triple point of the surface low with strong, rotating updrafts. Longevity was initially lacking with the storms, producing funnel clouds, brief tornadoes, and hail in southwest Iowa. As the cells moved northeast and matured, larger hail began to fall with golf ball sized hail falling in Adams county and baseball sized hail into Adair county. Following this period of large hail the storms produced a tornado which would remain on the ground for just over 70 miles, carving a path across central Iowa from southwest of Winterset to just northeast of Newton. The tornado peaked in Winterset, Iowa, producing EF-4 damage with wind speeds estimated near 170 mph. The tornado continued across the southern portion of the Des Moines metro area and to Newton. This is the furthest north EF-4 tornado in the CONUS this early in the year on record, the first EF-4 tornado in Iowa since October 4, 2013 which occurred in Woodbury and Cherokee Counties, and is the second longest tornado in Iowa since 1980, behind the longest occurring on June 7, 1984 at a length of 117 miles across southern Iowa. As the storm skimmed the southern Des Moines metro, cells across south central became tornadic, producing several destructive tornadoes including an EF-3 tornado in Chariton, Iowa. This heartbreaking day resulted in seven fatalities, six in Winterset and one in Chariton, making it the deadliest tornado outbreak in Iowa since 2008. At 15 tornadoes, this is also one of the earliest outbreaks of this magnitude to occur so early in the season.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado was the next in a series of tornadoes from the same supercell which tracked across central Iowa on this day.  It formed southwest of the intersection of 370th Street and H Avenue and moved northeast.  While remaining mostly over cropland and wooded areas, the tornado did impact a couple different residences with EF1 damage to outbuildings along Highway 63 south of Tama and then EF2 damage to a house on Highway E64 southeast of Tama where the roof was removed.  Several cars were also tossed around at this location.   The tornado then moved into the Iowa River valley producing tree damage with the tornado dissipating just shy of Highway 30 near P Avenue.

A passing cold front later in the day brought showers and thunderstorms, with a few storms becoming severe. Downed trees and wires from damaging wind gusts were most of the reports out of Northeastern Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm winds knocked down multiple trees and wires.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A quick-moving area of low pressure passed south of Pennsylvania on March 9, 2022, and progressed off the Delmarva Peninsula and out to sea. This system produced a swatch of 6+ inches of snow in less than 12 hours across portions of the northern mountains of Pennsylvania, with lesser snowfall amounts farther to the south and primarily rain (occasionally mixed with wet snow) in the Lower Susquehanna Valley.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A quick-hitting winter storm produced up to 6 inches of snow across Potter County in less than 12 hours on March 12, 2022.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As an upper trough moved eastward into New England on July 2, 2022, the eastern half of Pennsylvania remained in the right entrance region of the trough, promoting weak ascent in the atmosphere. A cold front slowly moved southeastward across Pennsylvania, with a prefrontal trough over the lower Susquehanna Valley acting as a primary trigger for afternoon convection. Several discrete and multicell thunderstorms developed within a narrow corridor around the prefrontal trough, in an environment with 2000 J/kg CAPE and up to 1200 J/kg of DCAPE. Deep layer 0-6 km shear of up to 35 kts combined with the instability to promote briefly rotating updrafts with transient supercell characteristics for at least one thunderstorm, which produced ping pong ball size hail. There were also several reports of damaging straight line winds associated with downbursts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm produced quarter to ping-pong ball sized hail in East Drumore Township.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front crossed Pennsylvania during the early morning hours of March 12, 2022. A few rain showers accompanied the front across the area, and then a wave of low pressure developed along the front as it slowly pulled east of central Pennsylvania. As steadier precipitation arrived, colder air arrived behind the front and changed the rain over to snow from northwest to southeast across the area into the mid-morning of March 12. A relatively short-lived period of moderate to heavy snow produced widespread 4 to 6 inches of snow, with localized amounts approaching 10 inches. Gusty northwest winds resulted in considerable blowing snow and reduced visibilities for many locations by the afternoon of March 12, as low pressure continued northeastward and rapidly intensified off the New England coast.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A winter storm produced 5 to 7 inches of snow across Perry County in less than 12 hours on March 12, 2022.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front crossed Pennsylvania during the early morning hours of March 12, 2022. A few rain showers accompanied the front across the area, and then a wave of low pressure developed along the front as it slowly pulled east of central Pennsylvania. As steadier precipitation arrived, colder air arrived behind the front and changed the rain over to snow from northwest to southeast across the area into the mid-morning of March 12. A relatively short-lived period of moderate to heavy snow produced widespread 4 to 6 inches of snow, with localized amounts approaching 10 inches. Gusty northwest winds resulted in considerable blowing snow and reduced visibilities for many locations by the afternoon of March 12, as low pressure continued northeastward and rapidly intensified off the New England coast.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A winter storm produced 5 to 7 inches of snow across Schuylkill County in less than 12 hours on March 12, 2022. This snow was accompanied and followed by winds gusting over 40 mph, which caused continued blowing and drifting snow through the day.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stalled frontal boundary south of the Mason-Dixon line returned northward as a warm front as low pressure pushed up the Ohio Valley during the evening of June 8, 2022. This system generated widespread showers and some strong thunderstorms across southwestern Pennsylvania, northern West Virginia, and western Maryland. Many of these storms were rotating in the vicinity of the warm front, and some produced sporadic wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing winds estimated between 75 and 85 mph produced wind damage in the Eagle Ridge housing development. Multiple homes in the Eagle Ridge housing development sustained minor structural damage ranging from sheds/outbuildings to roofs (shingles or fallen tree branches) and siding/downspouts. One residence received moderate damage due to a collapsed detached garage which also impacted vehicles that were parked underneath the garage and nearby. Several trees were also uprooted or knocked down. No injuries were reported. The damage was determined by an EMA/NWS coordinated damage assessment to have been straight-line in nature.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: There was barely a break between the exit of the earlier morning severe convection, and development of the next round during the later morning and early afternoon on May 30th across southeast South Dakota.  A series of impulses moved northeast during the day, with a leading strong wave moving out of Nebraska by early afternoon. Storms blossomed near a cold frontal boundary toward the James River Valley, despite the limited diurnal destabilization, due to steep mid-level lapse rates which brought MLCAPE up to 1500-2000J/kg in the warm sector. Strong mid-level winds led to long, linear hodographs, but strong deep-layer forcing eventually resulted in an evolution toward linear structures with mainly damaging wind.  Near the core of the upper level wave, a secondary band of thunderstorms developed across Nebraska during the late afternoon and raced northeastward through early evening, featuring mainly damaging wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very strong deep-layer shear developed as a result of an increase in the low-level jet and turning mid-level winds ahead of the approaching strong upper-level trough. A strong push of mid-level instability created up to 1000 J/kg MUCAPE, despite an environment with a strong sub-cloud dry layer. Storms moved rapidly northeast, with a cluster of hail producing storms in east central South Dakota. A second round of wind-producing storms erupted on the nose of the low-level jet across far northeast Nebraska, and translated quickly through southeast South Dakota into northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Three-inch diameter tree branches were downed by thunderstorm wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An amplified and vigorous upper level pattern pushed several weak disturbances northeast across the region during the overnight and early morning of May 30th. With ample elevated instability on the order of 2000-2500 J/kg available and effective shear of 35 to 45 knots, storms became severe across south central South Dakota and north central Nebraska and organized into a large scale QLCS as it moved east and northeast into Minnesota and Iowa late night. Several QLCS tornadoes developed from the Sioux Falls area eastward. Widespread winds of 60 to 90 mph caused scattered tree damage, with isolated pockets of more significant structural damage. Presidential Disaster Declarations were granted to Lyon, Rock, and Nobles Counties in Minnesota for damages to public infrastructure.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado spun up near the intersection of Fig Avenue and 140th Street.  On a northeastward track, the tornado impacted two farmsteads around a mile apart, with significant roof damage done to outbuildings at each location, as well as destruction of a  large grain bin.  The tornado tracked a few hundred yards beyond the final farm before dissipating in an open field. The estimated maximum wind was 90 mph and the average path width was 75 yards.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of thunderstorms focused near Cleveland became organized (into a squall line) the evening of June 1st and unleashed strong damaging wind north and west of Pittsburgh. The environment was prime for strong storms to occur: mean layer CAPE was near 1500 J/kg at the time of the squall line and effective bulk shear ranged between 30-35kts. Storms lost their intensity as they approached Pittsburgh and a gust front jetted out ahead of the line of convection, approaching an area that lacked robust instability.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter reported power lines down near Pulaski.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A volatile environment featured a warm front from parts of east central South Dakota into western Minnesota, with a dryline extending to the southwest into Nebraska. With a very strong wave moving northeast through Nebraska into a highly unstable and highly sheared environment, scattered storms initiated and quickly grew upscale to a broad linear structure with damaging winds. With crop development well behind schedule and many fields yet to be planted, there was ample dirt available to be lofted into the leading edge of the storms, which took on the characteristics of a haboob reducing visibility to near zero at the onset of high winds.||A broad swath of winds from 70 to 100 mph devastated much of southeast South Dakota, and portions of southwest Minnesota, northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, causing extensive tree and structural damage and scores of injuries. The highest observed wind gust was 107 mph near Tripp, SD. In addition, vehicles and high profile vehicles were blown off several roads, shutting down traffic on Interstates 29 and 90. Two (direct) fatalities occurred in vehicles impacted by debris as the storms moved into the Sioux Falls area. Power was disrupted in a widespread area, with estimates of over 45,000 customers impacted at one time. Many schools were closed due to damage and power issues. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong storms that produced damaging winds developed the evening of June 22, 2022. A broken line of showers and storms developed between Cleveland and Pittsburgh just before 3pm and continue to advances southeast along the axis of a trough entering from the north. Dry conditions under ridging hours ahead of the showers and storms helped prime the environment. Mean level CAPE before convective was between 3000-3500J/kg, and steep lapse rates near the surface (7.5 to 8.0C/km) help with strong damaging updrafts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down in East Allegheny.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system resulted in a northward push of warmth and moisture into the mid-upper Missouri River Basin during the late afternoon and evening of April 12th. Ample 0 to 6 km shear of 60 to 70 kts, combined with MLCAPE values of 1000-2500 J/kg resulted in a prime environment for severe thunderstorms. Severe hail averaging in size from quarters to ping-pong balls fell across portions of southeast South Dakota, southwest Minnesota, and northwest Iowa. Another cold front-induced line of convection developed later in the evening across eastern Nebraska and northwest Iowa, with the primary threat being damaging winds.||More widespread synoptic high winds followed the passage of a strong cold front. Peak wind gusts in excess of 58 mph occurred across much of southeast South Dakota and into portions of northwest Iowa.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A long-duration, multi-faceted winter storm hit northwestern Pennsylvania just before Christmas 2022 with extreme cold, strong winds, accumulating snow and extensive blowing and drifting of the snow that fell. An Arctic cold front swept east across northwestern Pennsylvania during the early morning hours of December 23rd. Low pressure along this front tracked over Lake Erie early in the morning on December 23rd and rapidly intensified through the day while slowly lifting northeast across Ontario. With the frontal passage rain changed to snow with temperatures dropping from the upper 30s and lower 40s to sub-zero in about 8 hours. The snow was generally light to moderate, but a brief period of heavier snow with rates of around one inch per hour lifted through during the morning hours December 23rd. The period of snow and rapidly falling temperatures led to a flash freeze and icy conditions on area roadways. While the falling snow became lighter through the afternoon hours of December 23rd, winds began increasing during the morning and gusted over 40 MPH through the day. Peak gusts of up to 55 MPH were measured near the Lake Erie shoreline. Peak gusts across the rest of northwestern Pennsylvania were generally 40-50 MPH. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front crossed Pennsylvania during the early morning hours of March 12, 2022. A few rain showers accompanied the front across the area, and then a wave of low pressure developed along the front as it slowly pulled east of central Pennsylvania. As steadier precipitation arrived, colder air arrived behind the front and changed the rain over to snow from northwest to southeast across the area into the mid-morning of March 12. A relatively short-lived period of moderate to heavy snow produced widespread 4 to 6 inches of snow, with localized amounts approaching 10 inches. Gusty northwest winds resulted in considerable blowing snow and reduced visibilities for many locations by the afternoon of March 12, as low pressure continued northeastward and rapidly intensified off the New England coast.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A winter storm produced 6 to 7 inches of snow across Clearfield County in less than 12 hours during the early morning hours of March 12, 2022. This snow was accompanied and followed by winds gusting over 40 mph, which caused continued blowing and drifting snow through the day.

There were several bowing segments within the QLCS, and there were a number of wind damage reports (and one quarter-sized hail report) that resulted.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing winds estimated near 60 mph produced multiple reports of trees down a couple miles northeast of Mifflintown.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing winds estimated near 60 mph knocked down multiple trees in Mahanoy City.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As a compact jet streak ejected out of a deep western U.S. trough, a strong area of low pressure developed and tracked northeast from Kansas to Iowa. Initial thermal profiles were warm enough to result in a brief period of light freezing rain before a transition to snow, but with generally light ice accumulation and little snow accumulation across northwest Iowa. A few rumbles of thunder were accompanied by small hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A period of light freezing rain in the afternoon resulted in up to one-tenth of an inch ice accumulation at Larchwood.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front pushed into an anomalously warm and humid airmass over central Pennsylvania during the afternoon of March 31, 2022, triggering a QLCS that stretched from the New York state line southward into Maryland. CAPE was relatively low (generally <500 J/kg), but shear was high. There were several bowing segments within the QLCS, and there were a number of wind damage reports (and one quarter-sized hail report) that resulted.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing winds estimated near 60 mph knocked down trees onto wires near Barlow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system rapidly intensified December 22nd to December 23rd as the center of the low moved from the Midwest across the Great Lakes. A flash freeze, strong wind gusts, and dangerously cold temperatures were recorded across the region. Record low maximum temperatures were broken at several climate sites. Widespread power outages were noted by utility companies, isolated areas experienced internal damage from frozen pipes,  and hazardous travel was noted due to a flash freeze (rain quickly changed to snow) with rapidly dropping temperatures.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A flash freeze created hazardous travel early Friday, December 23th, with a strong cold front. Temperatures dropped from the mid-40s to the single digits between 4:00am and 8am in Allegheny County. Precipitation started as rain and quickly switched to snow with the passage of the front. About an inch of snow fell by 7am on the December 23rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A storm brought an extended period of hazardous winter weather to northeast Iowa ahead of the Christmas holiday. Periods of snow fell from December 21st into the 23rd. Most accumulations were in the 2 to 5 inch range with the highest totals around 5 inches at Lock and Dam 10 near Guttenberg (Clayton County) and 4 inches north of Frankville (Winneshiek County). Strong winds of 30 to 45 mph from the 23rd into the 24th created blowing and drifting snow. Whiteouts were common and blizzard conditions occurred across Floyd, Chickasaw and Fayette County. Numerous rural roads were drifted shut across these counties. State snow plows were pulled off the roads across all of the region for the evening of the 23rd into the early morning of the 24th. The wind combined with an influx of arctic air to create dangerously cold wind chills from the 22nd into Christmas morning. Values of 25 to 40 below zero were common during this period with the lowest calculated wind chill of -43 near Monona (Clayton County).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: COOP and volunteer snow observers reported that 2 to 3 inches of snow fell across Allamakee County. The highest reported total was 2.5 inches near Monona and Postville. Strong winds with gusts of 25 to 40 mph created blowing and drifting snow with some occasional whiteouts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large winter system impacted Iowa and much of the Midwest in the days leading up to Christmas 2022. Snow began to fall across Iowa on the 21st and lasted through the morning of the 22nd, blanketing most of the state in a widespread depth of two to four inches. At the same time, temperature began to plummet with wind chills across the area dropping into the minus 30s and minus 40s by the morning of the 22nd. As the system began to shift east the tight pressure gradient and strong cold air advection allowed winds to increase, gusting to over 40 mph in many locations by the 23rd. A few places even recorded wind gusts of 50 to 58 mph. The strong winds and fresh snow resulted in blizzard conditions across portions of central and all of northern Iowa on the 23rd with visibility near zero. Winds gradually eased overnight with significant improvement to visibility by Christmas Eve morning. Conditions significantly impacted holiday travel with dozens of car accidents reported and a closure of interstate 35. This was a historic event. While extreme cold occurs with regularity in Iowa, the duration of this arctic outbreak set this event apart. The combination with blizzard conditions resulted in especially dangerous conditions putting anyone stranded at severe risk.

Widespread power outages were noted by utility companies, isolated areas experienced internal damage from frozen pipes,  and hazardous travel was noted due to a flash freeze (rain quickly changed to snow) with rapidly dropping temperatures.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A flash freeze created hazardous travel early Friday, December 23th, with a strong cold front. Temperatures dropped from the mid-40s to the single digits between 7:00am and 10am in Forest County. Precipitation started as rain and quickly switched to snow with the passage of the front. About an inch of snow fell by 7am on the December 23rd.

The entire region exceeded Wind Chill Warning criteria for multiple days and most locations bottomed out between 45 below and 55 below zero. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chills dropped as low as -48F near Storm Lake (AWOS site KSLB) and 2 miles northeast of Truesdale (Iowa Road Weather Information System site RSLI4), and -47 1 mile south of Newell (Iowa mesonet site NWLI4).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A storm brought an extended period of hazardous winter weather to northeast Iowa ahead of the Christmas holiday. Periods of snow fell from December 21st into the 23rd. Most accumulations were in the 2 to 5 inch range with the highest totals around 5 inches at Lock and Dam 10 near Guttenberg (Clayton County) and 4 inches north of Frankville (Winneshiek County). Strong winds of 30 to 45 mph from the 23rd into the 24th created blowing and drifting snow. Whiteouts were common and blizzard conditions occurred across Floyd, Chickasaw and Fayette County. Numerous rural roads were drifted shut across these counties. State snow plows were pulled off the roads across all of the region for the evening of the 23rd into the early morning of the 24th. The wind combined with an influx of arctic air to create dangerously cold wind chills from the 22nd into Christmas morning. Values of 25 to 40 below zero were common during this period with the lowest calculated wind chill of -43 near Monona (Clayton County).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: COOP and volunteer snow observers reported that 2 to 3 inches of snow fell across Floyd County. The highest reported total was 3 inches near Nashua. Strong winds with gusts of 25 to 45 mph created blowing and drifting snow with blizzard conditions occurring from the late morning into the afternoon of the 23rd. The highest record gust was 49 mph by the automated weather observing equipment at the Charles City airport. County snow plows were pulled off the roads on the 23rd and emergency management recommended no travel in the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large winter system impacted Iowa and much of the Midwest in the days leading up to Christmas 2022. Snow began to fall across Iowa on the 21st and lasted through the morning of the 22nd, blanketing most of the state in a widespread depth of two to four inches. At the same time, temperature began to plummet with wind chills across the area dropping into the minus 30s and minus 40s by the morning of the 22nd. As the system began to shift east the tight pressure gradient and strong cold air advection allowed winds to increase, gusting to over 40 mph in many locations by the 23rd. A few places even recorded wind gusts of 50 to 58 mph. The strong winds and fresh snow resulted in blizzard conditions across portions of central and all of northern Iowa on the 23rd with visibility near zero. Winds gradually eased overnight with significant improvement to visibility by Christmas Eve morning. Conditions significantly impacted holiday travel with dozens of car accidents reported and a closure of interstate 35. This was a historic event. While extreme cold occurs with regularity in Iowa, the duration of this arctic outbreak set this event apart. The combination with blizzard conditions resulted in especially dangerous conditions putting anyone stranded at severe risk.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong winter storm brought widespread snow to the region Thursday, with amounts  between 1 to 4 inches.  Some higher totals near 6 inches were reported in eastern Linn and Cedar counties.  Strong winds also accompanied the snow, which caused significant blowing and drifting, especially in rural areas.  Many accidents were reported on Interstate 80, causing frequent backups.  Even stronger winds were observed on Friday across the area.  Wind gusts between 40-50 mph were common, creating ground blizzard conditions primarily along and north of Interstate 80.||Additionally, temperatures dropped sharply behind the arctic cold front on Thursday and continued to fall throughout the day.  Single digit temperatures with wind chills between -20 and -40 degrees were common.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Freshly fallen snow, combined with strong northwest winds sustained between 20 to 30 knots and gusts up to 37 knots during the afternoon produced blizzard conditions across the county.  Numerous spotter reports, web and snowplow cameras showed blizzard conditions outside of cities and towns.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm resulted in warm-air advection precipitation lifting from south to north across northeast Nebraska, northwest Iowa, southeast South Dakota, and southwest Minnesota during the afternoon and evening of December 8th and continuing into the early morning hours of December 9th. Initially, the precipitation fell as light freezing drizzle or rain, but quickly transitioned to snow. While light to moderate snow persisted for much of the evening, heavy snow fell in a narrow convective-like band where rates exceeded 2 to 3 inches per hour. Thunder-snow was also observed with very large (plate-like) aggregates. Within this band, which stretched from near Mitchell to Sioux Falls to Spencer, snowfall amounts exceeded 6 inches with some isolated areas picking up 9 to 10 inches. Light winds persisted throughout the event, so reductions in visibility were related to the snowfall rate.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light freezing rain or drizzle resulted in a glaze of ice. Precipitation then quickly transitioned to snow, accumulating to 6.3 inches at the CoCoRaHS site 1.2 miles north-northeast of Larchwood and 3.7 inches at the COOP site in Rock Rapids. Other public reports across the county ranged from 6 to 8 inches.

Many accidents were reported on Interstate 80, causing frequent backups.  Even stronger winds were observed on Friday across the area.  Wind gusts between 40-50 mph were common, creating ground blizzard conditions primarily along and north of Interstate 80.||Additionally, temperatures dropped sharply behind the arctic cold front on Thursday and continued to fall throughout the day.  Single digit temperatures with wind chills between -20 and -40 degrees were common.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The COOP Observer in Clinton reported 3.0 inches of snow. A trained spotter northeast of Clinton reported 1.9 inches of snow. Winds increased on the 22nd with gusts over 40 to 50 MPH which produced blizzard conditions especially in rural and open areas for several hours. The wind chill values at the Clinton Airport was as cold as -30.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A storm brought an extended period of hazardous winter weather to northeast Iowa ahead of the Christmas holiday. Periods of snow fell from December 21st into the 23rd. Most accumulations were in the 2 to 5 inch range with the highest totals around 5 inches at Lock and Dam 10 near Guttenberg (Clayton County) and 4 inches north of Frankville (Winneshiek County). Strong winds of 30 to 45 mph from the 23rd into the 24th created blowing and drifting snow. Whiteouts were common and blizzard conditions occurred across Floyd, Chickasaw and Fayette County. Numerous rural roads were drifted shut across these counties. State snow plows were pulled off the roads across all of the region for the evening of the 23rd into the early morning of the 24th. The wind combined with an influx of arctic air to create dangerously cold wind chills from the 22nd into Christmas morning. Values of 25 to 40 below zero were common during this period with the lowest calculated wind chill of -43 near Monona (Clayton County).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The combination of arctic air and wind gusts of 25 to 45 mph created wind chills of 20 to 40 below zero across Chickasaw County. The lowest calculated wind chill was 41 below at a mesonet site in New Hampton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large winter system impacted Iowa and much of the Midwest in the days leading up to Christmas 2022. Snow began to fall across Iowa on the 21st and lasted through the morning of the 22nd, blanketing most of the state in a widespread depth of two to four inches. At the same time, temperature began to plummet with wind chills across the area dropping into the minus 30s and minus 40s by the morning of the 22nd. As the system began to shift east the tight pressure gradient and strong cold air advection allowed winds to increase, gusting to over 40 mph in many locations by the 23rd. A few places even recorded wind gusts of 50 to 58 mph. The strong winds and fresh snow resulted in blizzard conditions across portions of central and all of northern Iowa on the 23rd with visibility near zero. Winds gradually eased overnight with significant improvement to visibility by Christmas Eve morning. Conditions significantly impacted holiday travel with dozens of car accidents reported and a closure of interstate 35. This was a historic event. While extreme cold occurs with regularity in Iowa, the duration of this arctic outbreak set this event apart. The combination with blizzard conditions resulted in especially dangerous conditions putting anyone stranded at severe risk.

A low pressure system rapidly intensified December 22nd to December 23rd as the center of the low moved from the Midwest across the Great Lakes. A flash freeze, strong wind gusts, and dangerously cold temperatures were recorded across the region. Record low maximum temperatures were broken at several climate sites. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm resulted in warm-air advection precipitation lifting from south to north across northeast Nebraska, northwest Iowa, southeast South Dakota, and southwest Minnesota during the afternoon and evening of December 8th and continuing into the early morning hours of December 9th. Initially, the precipitation fell as light freezing drizzle or rain, but quickly transitioned to snow. While light to moderate snow persisted for much of the evening, heavy snow fell in a narrow convective-like band where rates exceeded 2 to 3 inches per hour. Thunder-snow was also observed with very large (plate-like) aggregates. Within this band, which stretched from near Mitchell to Sioux Falls to Spencer, snowfall amounts exceeded 6 inches with some isolated areas picking up 9 to 10 inches. Light winds persisted throughout the event, so reductions in visibility were related to the snowfall rate.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light freezing rain or drizzle resulted in a glaze of ice. Precipitation then quickly transitioned to snow, accumulating to 7.7 inches at the COOP site at Spirit Lake. Other public reports across the county ranged from 6 to 9 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a wintry mix of precipitation on December 12 and a warmup to allow mainly rainfall on December 13, temperatures fell with a change to snow. Snow and stronger winds began earlier in the day December 14 west of the James River, with the transition to snow mainly later into the early morning hours of December 15 toward Interstate 29. With northwest winds gusting at times from 40 to 55 mph, several areas exhibited periods of blizzard conditions on the 15th and early on the 16th. The heaviest snowfall occurred from the James River Valley westward, where up to 10 to 17 inches was common. Amounts decreased toward the south and east, with less than 3 inches in far southeast South Dakota, northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow developed early on December 15, with strong and gusty winds developing shortly after this time. Consistent visibility of one-quarter mile occurred from late morning through the afternoon, with a peak wind gust reaching 39 mph at the Iowa State Road Weather Information System site DONI4 near Doon. Snowfall totaled 3.3 inches at COOP site RKRI4 in Rock Rapids.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a 2 to 4 inch fluffy snow accumulation across most of northwest Iowa on December 21 and 22, a strong Arctic front surged through the area with strong and gusty northwest winds from 35 to 55 mph, creating widespread whiteout conditions. Most county, state, and federal highways were either impassable or with travel not recommended.  Drifts as high as 5 to 10 feet were documented through social media.  Numerous accidents and stranded vehicles complicated recovery efforts. School, county, and state operations were cancelled for several days when conditions were coupled with life-threatening wind chills. Winds resulted in spotty power outages around the Iowa Great Lakes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Northwest winds gusted to 52 mph at Automated Weather Observing System site KSLB near Storm Lake and 48 mph at Iowa Road Weather Information System site RSLI4 near Truesdale, resulting in frequent whiteout conditions.

Ice accumulated in the ridges of the Laurel Highlands and along our northeastern county warning area with surface temperatures below freezing due to surface winds prevailing from the east. Freezing rain eventually turned to rain as the 50kt low-level jet shifts east into western Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A prolong period of freezing rain on the morning of December 15th in the ridges of Westmoreland County created three tenths of ice to accumulate on surfaces. Highest report was made in Wilpen, PA.

While light to moderate snow persisted for much of the evening, heavy snow fell in a narrow convective-like band where rates exceeded 2 to 3 inches per hour. Thunder-snow was also observed with very large (plate-like) aggregates. Within this band, which stretched from near Mitchell to Sioux Falls to Spencer, snowfall amounts exceeded 6 inches with some isolated areas picking up 9 to 10 inches. Light winds persisted throughout the event, so reductions in visibility were related to the snowfall rate.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light freezing rain or drizzle resulted in a glaze of ice. Precipitation then quickly transitioned to snow, accumulating to 6.8 inches at the COOP site in Sanborn, 5.0 inches at the COOP site in Primghar, and 5.0 inches at the COOP site in Sheldon. Other public reports across the county ranged from 5 to 8 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong winter storm brought widespread snow to the region Thursday, with amounts  between 1 to 4 inches.  Some higher totals near 6 inches were reported in eastern Linn and Cedar counties.  Strong winds also accompanied the snow, which caused significant blowing and drifting, especially in rural areas.  Many accidents were reported on Interstate 80, causing frequent backups.  Even stronger winds were observed on Friday across the area.  Wind gusts between 40-50 mph were common, creating ground blizzard conditions primarily along and north of Interstate 80.||Additionally, temperatures dropped sharply behind the arctic cold front on Thursday and continued to fall throughout the day.  Single digit temperatures with wind chills between -20 and -40 degrees were common.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall reports from the previous day ranged from 3 to 4 inches of snow. Peak wind gusts ranged from 45 to 55 MPH. There was a measured gusts of 52 MPH at the Independence Airport as well as CWOP site in Independence.  This led to widespread blowing and drifting snow across the area resulting in blizzard conditions.  Wind chills were also dangerously cold with a minimum wind chill at the Independence of -32.
