EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a wintry mix of precipitation on December 12 and a warmup to allow mainly rainfall on December 13, temperatures fell with a change to snow. Snow and stronger winds began earlier in the day December 14 west of the James River, with the transition to snow mainly later into the early morning hours of December 15 toward Interstate 29. With northwest winds gusting at times from 40 to 55 mph, several areas exhibited periods of blizzard conditions on the 15th and early on the 16th. The heaviest snowfall occurred from the James River Valley westward, where up to 10 to 17 inches was common. Amounts decreased toward the south and east, with less than 3 inches in far southeast South Dakota, northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow developed early on December 15, with strong and gusty winds developing shortly after this time. Consistent visibility of one-quarter mile occurred from late morning through early afternoon, with a peak wind gust reaching 41 mph at the Iowa State Road Weather Information System site RTNI4 near Orange City. Snowfall totaled 3.7 inches at COOP site ORCI4 in Orange City.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a 2 to 4 inch fluffy snow accumulation across most of northwest Iowa on December 21 and 22, a strong Arctic front surged through the area with strong and gusty northwest winds from 35 to 55 mph, creating widespread whiteout conditions. Most county, state, and federal highways were either impassable or with travel not recommended.  Drifts as high as 5 to 10 feet were documented through social media.  Numerous accidents and stranded vehicles complicated recovery efforts. School, county, and state operations were cancelled for several days when conditions were coupled with life-threatening wind chills. Winds resulted in spotty power outages around the Iowa Great Lakes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Northwest winds gusted to 40 mph at Automated Weather Observing System site KCKP at Cherokee, resulting in frequent whiteout conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A storm brought an extended period of hazardous winter weather to northeast Iowa ahead of the Christmas holiday. Periods of snow fell from December 21st into the 23rd. Most accumulations were in the 2 to 5 inch range with the highest totals around 5 inches at Lock and Dam 10 near Guttenberg (Clayton County) and 4 inches north of Frankville (Winneshiek County). Strong winds of 30 to 45 mph from the 23rd into the 24th created blowing and drifting snow. Whiteouts were common and blizzard conditions occurred across Floyd, Chickasaw and Fayette County. Numerous rural roads were drifted shut across these counties. State snow plows were pulled off the roads across all of the region for the evening of the 23rd into the early morning of the 24th. The wind combined with an influx of arctic air to create dangerously cold wind chills from the 22nd into Christmas morning. Values of 25 to 40 below zero were common during this period with the lowest calculated wind chill of -43 near Monona (Clayton County).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The combination of arctic air and wind gusts of 25 to 45 mph created wind chills of 20 to 40 below zero across Winneshiek County. The lowest calculated wind chill was 41 below at a mesonet site near Jackson Junction.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large winter system impacted Iowa and much of the Midwest in the days leading up to Christmas 2022. Snow began to fall across Iowa on the 21st and lasted through the morning of the 22nd, blanketing most of the state in a widespread depth of two to four inches. At the same time, temperature began to plummet with wind chills across the area dropping into the minus 30s and minus 40s by the morning of the 22nd. As the system began to shift east the tight pressure gradient and strong cold air advection allowed winds to increase, gusting to over 40 mph in many locations by the 23rd. A few places even recorded wind gusts of 50 to 58 mph. The strong winds and fresh snow resulted in blizzard conditions across portions of central and all of northern Iowa on the 23rd with visibility near zero. Winds gradually eased overnight with significant improvement to visibility by Christmas Eve morning. Conditions significantly impacted holiday travel with dozens of car accidents reported and a closure of interstate 35. This was a historic event. While extreme cold occurs with regularity in Iowa, the duration of this arctic outbreak set this event apart. The combination with blizzard conditions resulted in especially dangerous conditions putting anyone stranded at severe risk.

A strong and slow moving upper-level low centered in the northern Plains impacted portions of the Ohio River Valley with the passage of the warm front on December 15th. Ice accumulated in the ridges of the Laurel Highlands and along our northeastern county warning area with surface temperatures below freezing due to surface winds prevailing from the east. Freezing rain eventually turned to rain as the 50kt low-level jet shifts east into western Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple reports of ice, up to a tenth of an inch, in Clarion County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system rapidly intensified December 22nd to December 23rd as the center of the low moved from the Midwest across the Great Lakes. A flash freeze, strong wind gusts, and dangerously cold temperatures were recorded across the region. Record low maximum temperatures were broken at several climate sites. Widespread power outages were noted by utility companies, isolated areas experienced internal damage from frozen pipes,  and hazardous travel was noted due to a flash freeze (rain quickly changed to snow) with rapidly dropping temperatures.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dangerous wind chills accompanied a low pressure system on December 23th. Lowest wind chill values occurred early afternoon on December 23rd, temperatures were below zero and gusts were 30 to 35mph. Minimum wind chill values across western PA were near -30F.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm resulted in warm-air advection precipitation lifting from south to north across northeast Nebraska, northwest Iowa, southeast South Dakota, and southwest Minnesota during the afternoon and evening of December 8th and continuing into the early morning hours of December 9th. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After a 2 to 4 inch fluffy snow accumulation across most of northwest Iowa on December 21 and 22, a strong Arctic front surged through the area with strong and gusty northwest winds from 35 to 55 mph, creating widespread whiteout conditions. Most county, state, and federal highways were either impassable or with travel not recommended.  Drifts as high as 5 to 10 feet were documented through social media.  Numerous accidents and stranded vehicles complicated recovery efforts. School, county, and state operations were cancelled for several days when conditions were coupled with life-threatening wind chills. Winds resulted in spotty power outages around the Iowa Great Lakes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Northwest winds gusted to 55 mph at Automated Weather Observing System site KSXK near Maurice and 46 mph at personal weather station FW6302 near Hawarden, resulting in frequent whiteout conditions.

The combination with blizzard conditions resulted in especially dangerous conditions putting anyone stranded at severe risk.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A storm brought an extended period of hazardous winter weather to northeast Iowa ahead of the Christmas holiday. Periods of snow fell from December 21st into the 23rd. Most accumulations were in the 2 to 5 inch range with the highest totals around 5 inches at Lock and Dam 10 near Guttenberg (Clayton County) and 4 inches north of Frankville (Winneshiek County). Strong winds of 30 to 45 mph from the 23rd into the 24th created blowing and drifting snow. Whiteouts were common and blizzard conditions occurred across Floyd, Chickasaw and Fayette County. Numerous rural roads were drifted shut across these counties. State snow plows were pulled off the roads across all of the region for the evening of the 23rd into the early morning of the 24th. The wind combined with an influx of arctic air to create dangerously cold wind chills from the 22nd into Christmas morning. Values of 25 to 40 below zero were common during this period with the lowest calculated wind chill of -43 near Monona (Clayton County).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The combination of arctic air and wind gusts of 25 to 45 mph created wind chills of 20 to 40 below zero across Fayette County. The lowest calculated wind chill was 42 below at the Oelwein airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A complex winter storm moved through Northeastern Pennsylvania on the 15th and 16th. Precipitation started out as freezing mix for some areas and snow for others. Any mix became mostly snow during the day of the 15th. Travel conditions became hazardous, especially during the evening commute, as snow accumulated on roadways. Some locations received a break from the snow overnight before it picked back up on the 16th due to a storm moving north along the Atlantic coast. Snow came to an end early on 17th. While most of the highest snowfall totals were east of I-81, there were locations west that also received significant snowfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow accumulated between 4 and 8 inches.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado developed near Overton Road and 286th Street in Harrison County Iowa. The tornado moved rapidly to the east where it made a direct impact on a home. At this location, the home roof was removed, windows broken, siding ruined, numerous trees snapped, a shed was demolished, and numerous items were thrown up to a half mile downstream. The convergent damage pattern at this location, eyewitness reports of wind direction, along with the 80-yard-wide path of more intense damage gives great confidence that this was a tornado. Winds at this location were estimated at 120 mph based on damage. The tornado moved quickly southeast, causing substantial tree damage with snapped trunks being common along the continued 50 to 100 yard wide track. The tornado moved through neighborhood of acreages along Quentin trail where it snapped many trees but moved in between the homes. The track then became more intermittent for a couple miles before it partially removed the roof of a home along 296th Street and caused additional narrow tree damage for the next two miles. The final damage point that was pretty clearly tornado damage was near 305th and Upton where 3 grain bins were crumpled and blown downstream and a machine shed sustained substantial damage. Beyond this point, the tree damage was sporadic and more evident of the larger scale wind field. Should also note that to the west of this tornado track, there was a debris signature evident on radar, but the damage was much more consistent with a focused downburst or series of downbursts that moved up from the Missouri Valley into the Loess Hills and may have helped to loft light leafy debris. This downburst likely led to the development of the eventual tornado.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A rapidly strengthening storm developed across the Northern Plains and into the western Great Lakes on March 16-17. An initial band of precipitation developed during the early morning hours of March 16 across northwest Iowa in the form of light rain or light freezing rain. However, a sharp fall in temperatures by midday and early afternoon forced a change to a few hours of snowfall accompanied by increasing northerly wind. Snow cover prior to the event was limited to areas north of Highway 18, where impacts from snow and blowing snow with winds of 45 to 55 mph were greatest during the afternoon of March 16, and again briefly on Friday, March 17 when reinvigorated winds brought very brief visibility of a quarter mile or less.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief period of light freezing rain resulted in a glaze of icing at the COOP site at Spencer. Northerly wind increased by the afternoon with gusts as high as 60 mph at Automated Surface Observing System site KSPW near Spencer.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Dense fog developed across portions of eastern Iowa overnight on the 9th and into the 10th, with visibilities to a quarter mile at times through the mid morning. Freezing fog resulted in slippery pavement. Early in the morning, a crash resulted on Interstate 80 due to ice covered roads. This incident led to two fatalities and several injuries.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Iowa State Patrol responded to a crash due to ice-covered roads, caused by overnight freezing fog and drizzle. A semi truck driver lost control of their vehicle and jackknifed on Interstate 80, which led to two fatalities and several injuries. Total number of injuries are unknown. 16 total cars were involved in the pile-up that morning.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large low pressure system spun northeast across Iowa on January 16, 2023, drawing mild temperatures northward into the area and sparking some showers and thunderstorms over portions of eastern Iowa.  Temperatures increased into the upper 40s to low 60s in parts of east central and southeast Iowa by early afternoon.  One storm ended up becoming severe, producing two tornadoes between 2 PM and 3 PM CST.   The first tornado touched down just northeast of Williamsburg, IA and the second one briefly touched down north of Ely, IA.  Some large hail up to the size of quarters was reported in Homestead, IA from this storm at 2:24 PM.  Several other areas that the storm tracked over reported hail covering the ground. These were the first tornadoes reported in Iowa in the month of January since January 24, 1967.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Nickel to quarter size hail covering the ground.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Increasing warm advection brought a period of freezing rain to northwest Iowa on January 2, which was reinvigorated by convection early on January 3. The most significant ice accumulations in excess of one-quarter inch occurred toward Highway 71, with lesser amounts to the west. Impacts were lessened by air temperatures which climbed to near or above freezing after the initial push of freezing rain. Colder air eventually resulted in a changeover to snow during January 3, with a band of heavy snowfall across far northern portions of northwest Iowa and rates up to 1 to 2 inches per hour during the early morning and midday hours. Roads in far northwest Iowa were closed or impassable during the height of the event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Freezing rain resulted in ice accumulations of almost one-half inch at Spencer. Cooler air changed precipitation to snow during the afternoon of January 3, which resulted in an accumulation of 3.7 inches at Spencer on top of the prior ice.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Persistent fog from the morning into the early afternoon of January 11 resulted in long periods of visibility less than one-quarter mile, as well as deposition of frost on roadways.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severely limited visibility and frosty roadways contributed to a two-vehicle accident at the intersection of U.S. Highway 59 and 20 just south of Holstein. An indirect fatality occurred to the driver of a car when it was hit broadside by a semi-truck upon entering the roadway after a stop at the intersection.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Increasing warm advection brought a period of freezing rain to northwest Iowa on January 2, which was reinvigorated by convection early on January 3. Impacts were lessened by air temperatures which climbed to near or above freezing after the initial push of freezing rain. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Deep moisture out of the Gulf was transported all the way to Iowa ahead of a deep, negatively tilted trough across the Rockies. Across Iowa, this resulted in a mixed precipitation event across the state with over an inch of rain across central to southern Iowa. Into northern Iowa the thermal profile cooled and mixed precipitation was reported, including snow, graupel, and freezing rain. Within an axis of colder air, freezing rain accumulated, especially on vegetation and elevated surfaces. Light snow accumulation of up to two inches and ice formed, glazing up to nearly half an inch was across parts of northwest Iowa. Temperatures warmed quickly after sunrise on the 3rd, helping to mitigate impacts from the wintry precipitation.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two inches of snow followed by nearly a half inch of ice accumulation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A long-duration winter storm developed across northwest Iowa on February 21, with waves of heavier snowfall across the region as winds increased to a gusty 30 to 50 mph. Blizzard conditions developed during the afternoon of February 22, with strong winds lingering into the midday hours of February 23. During the event, widespread blowing and drifting snowfall led to the closure of Interstate 90, as well as Interstate 29 north of Sioux Falls. Travel was not recommended in numerous counties, with schools and county/state offices closed due to the hazardous conditions. Total snowfall varied from around an inch near Highway 20 to around 10 inches near the Minnesota border.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level wave lifted out of the southwestern U.S. and closed off moving across Iowa by early on January 19. A band of snow developed within the leading warm advection zone from northern Nebraska to northern Iowa by late afternoon on January 18, and with unstable conditions near the frontal axis, the band evolved into a more narrow zone of intense snowfall into the overnight hours. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Increasing warm advection brought a period of freezing rain to northwest Iowa on January 2, which was reinvigorated by convection early on January 3. The most significant ice accumulations in excess of one-quarter inch occurred toward Highway 71, with lesser amounts to the west. Impacts were lessened by air temperatures which climbed to near or above freezing after the initial push of freezing rain. Colder air eventually resulted in a changeover to snow during January 3, with a band of heavy snowfall across far northern portions of northwest Iowa and rates up to 1 to 2 inches per hour during the early morning and midday hours. Roads in far northwest Iowa were closed or impassable during the height of the event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: After a period of light freezing rain with an accumulation up to a quarter inch near Hartley, heavy snowfall developed at times during the morning of January 3 with a two-day total of 5.6 inches at Sanborn and 5.0 inches at Sheldon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm front remained relatively stationary across the Upper Ohio Valley on January 3rd. An anomalously moist and warm air mass surged northward into the zone of convergence associated with the boundary, and combined with elevated instability to create enhanced rainfall rates.  In southwest Pennsylvania, Greene and Fayette Counties received the brunt of the rainfall, with storm total amounts of 1.5 to 2 inches in some cases. This rain led to some relatively minor road flooding reports.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minor flooding was reported on Iowa Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A long-duration winter storm developed across northwest Iowa on February 21, with waves of heavier snowfall across the region as winds increased to a gusty 30 to 50 mph. Blizzard conditions developed during the afternoon of February 22, with strong winds lingering into the midday hours of February 23. During the event, widespread blowing and drifting snowfall led to the closure of Interstate 90, as well as Interstate 29 north of Sioux Falls. Travel was not recommended in numerous counties, with schools and county/state offices closed due to the hazardous conditions. Total snowfall varied from around an inch near Highway 20 to around 10 inches near the Minnesota border.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Over the two-day period, snowfall accumulated to 5.1 inches at Primghar and 5.0 inches at Sheldon.  Whiteout conditions became widespread, especially in rural areas, due to winds which peaked at 44 mph at Sheldon.

However, northwest Iowa did not escape strong northwest winds which reached a gusty 40 to 60 mph, and many areas found considerable drifting of earlier snowfall along and north of Iowa Highway 3.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sustained winds reached 30 to 39 mph, with gusts as high as 46 mph at Iowa Department of Transportation Mesonet site RSYI4 near Sibley.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deeper than average snow pack from northern Minnesota and northern Wisconsin underwent a rapid melt through much of April from unseasonably warm temperatures and multiple rain events. This resulted in increased water levels and significant flooding for the entire length of the local Mississippi River, with most sites climbing to their third to fifth highest crests on record. In response to the widespread flooding, the Governor of Iowa issued a Proclamation of Disaster Emergency for counties along the Mississippi River. Initial flood warnings were issued in mid April with peak stages realized towards late April. The highest above flood stage was Guttenberg Dam at 6.91 ft over flood stage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Significant upstream runoff from the combination of rainfall and melting snow pushed the Mississippi River at Guttenberg into flood stage on April 18th. The crest of 20.98 ft on April 28th was 5.98 ft over flood stage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Intermittent light snow from  Saturday November 25th through Sunday November 26th resulted in slippery road conditions for the busy Thanksgiving holiday travel weekend. Law enforcement and broadcast media reported widespread vehicle incidents through the weekend. While snowfall rates remained under 0.1 inches per hour for most of the weekend, a scattered increase to 0.25 inches per hour Sunday evening temporarily reduced visibilities in spots. The longer duration resulted in a widespread 1.0 to 2.0 inches of overall accumulations by Sunday night. Highest snowfall reports were 2.8 inches near Strawberry Point (Clayton County) and 2.0 inches near Harpers Ferry (Allamakee County), Elkader (Clayton County), and the Town of Fayette (Fayette County).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Volunteer observers reported 1.3 to 2.0 inches of snowfall across Allamakee County with the highest amount reported near Harpers Ferry.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large and unseasonably warm system brought showers and thunderstorms to the state. Over an inch of rain fell across much of Iowa. In northern Iowa, this was on top of a snowpack of two to four inches. The quick rain on top of frozen group resulted in runoff sufficient to send the Winnebago River at Mason City into minor river flooding. The river exceeded minor flood stage and quickly crested the morning of February 27th before falling back below flood stage the morning of February 28th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: River entered flood state at 430am LST on the 27th of February, crested at 11.24 ft at 630am LST on February 27th, and fell below flood stage at 430am LST on February 28th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A rapidly strengthening storm developed across the Northern Plains and into the western Great Lakes on March 16-17. An initial band of precipitation developed during the early morning hours of March 16 across northwest Iowa in the form of light rain or light freezing rain. However, a sharp fall in temperatures by midday and early afternoon forced a change to a few hours of snowfall accompanied by increasing northerly wind. Snow cover prior to the event was limited to areas north of Highway 18, where impacts from snow and blowing snow with winds of 45 to 55 mph were greatest during the afternoon of March 16, and again briefly on Friday, March 17 when reinvigorated winds brought very brief visibility of a quarter mile or less.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief period of light freezing rain resulted in a glaze of icing, prior to a period of snowfall that accumulated to 0.5 inches at a CoCoRaHS site near Spirit Lake. Northerly wind increased by the afternoon of March 16 with gusts as high as 46 mph at personal weather stations EW9051 near Spirit Lake and FW7399 at Terril, resulting in brief visibility reduction to around one-half to one mile. After winds decreased overnight and early morning of March 17 with minimal impacts, winds increased again during the later morning and afternoon with frequent convective snow showers that briefly reduced visibility at times to one mile or less.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An occluded surface low meandered near the eastern shore of Lake Superior during the late morning through early evening of the 12th. Multiple multicell thunderstorms and a supercell thunderstorm occurred ahead of the cold front in northwest PA. These storms produced small hail, damaging convective gusts, and a tornado in a warm sector comprised of moderate to strong MUCAPE and effective bulk shear, respectively, mixed-layer lifting condensation levels near 750 to 1500 meters AGL, and strong surface-based effective storm-relative helicity near 150 meters squared per second squared.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to nickel-size in Spartansburg.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Light drizzle and freezing drizzle during the afternoon and evening of March 8th gradually mixed in with and transitioned to a light, long-duration snowfall through the day on March 9th in response to increasing 850 hPa warm air advection and low-level saturation. Ice accumulations were a glaze at best given warmer ground temperatures and total snowfall ranged from 1 to 5 inches across the region. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, an occluded low moved northeastward from southwestern Lower MI to central Lake Huron during the late morning through early evening of the 25th. Simultaneously, the accompanying warm front decelerated as it moved northeastward across northeast OH, into northwest PA, and toward the southwest corner of western New York. The low's trailing cold front swept eastward across northern OH and eventually overtook the warm front in northwest PA.||Clusters of multicell showers and thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts along the warm front and ahead of the cold front in northwest PA during the early to mid-afternoon. Moderate to strong effective bulk shear, weak MUCAPE, steep low-level lapse rates, and sizable DCAPE in the warm sector allowed precipitation associated with the surface-based and low-topped convection to be very efficient at transporting much stronger flow just aloft down to the surface. Some of the straight-line convective wind damage was associated with a brief microburst in Venango Township, Crawford County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees downed in Springfield Township (i.e. about six-miles west of Platea).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure tracked from the Lower Mississippi Valley on the morning of the 3rd towards the northeast U.S. coast on the morning of the 4th. Ahead of the low, ideal conditions for enhanced downslope wind existed along west-facing slopes of Indiana, Westmoreland and Fayette Counties, as strong southeast flow underneath an inversion at ridgetop accelerated as it progressed downslope, creating many measured wind gusts of 50 to 60 MPH on the 3rd.  Localized 70 MPH wind, although not measured, likely occurred as well.  Damage was most concentrated along the west-facing slopes of Fayette and Westmoreland, with many reports of tree and structural damage. Power outages were also widespread, with over 28% of Fayette County out at one point during the event. A Declaration of Disaster Emergency was issued for the county in the wake of the wind at noon on the 4th, with the city of Connellsville also issuing a local declaration.||Incidents of wind damage were more isolated in other portions of southwest Pennsylvania,  as wind gusts were slightly less severe, generally topping out at around 50 MPH.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread tree and power line damage was noted in Ohiopyle, and a road closure in Chalkhill was also attributed to downed trees and power lines.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the surface, an occluded low moved northeastward from southwestern Lower MI to central Lake Huron during the late morning through early evening of the 25th. Simultaneously, the accompanying warm front decelerated as it moved northeastward across northeast OH, into northwest PA, and toward the southwest corner of western New York. The low's trailing cold front swept eastward across northern OH and eventually overtook the warm front in northwest PA.||Clusters of multicell showers and thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts along the warm front and ahead of the cold front in northwest PA during the early to mid-afternoon. Moderate to strong effective bulk shear, weak MUCAPE, steep low-level lapse rates, and sizable DCAPE in the warm sector allowed precipitation associated with the surface-based and low-topped convection to be very efficient at transporting much stronger flow just aloft down to the surface. Some of the straight-line convective wind damage was associated with a brief microburst in Venango Township, Crawford County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NWS storm damage survey found evidence of a brief microburst in Venango Township. The maximum damage path width was 30 yards and estimated peak gusts were 100 mph. This microburst began one-mile north of Venango, just west of Plank Road, where numerous trees were snapped 10 to 30 feet above the ground. As the microburst advanced east-northeastward, it blew-out windows and tore off the sheet metal roof of a fishing camp, blew a tree onto a home, and blew debris onto an RV trailer. These structures were located between Plank Road and French Creek. Snapped trees and debris were strewn in the same direction, from WSW to ENE, indicative of straight-line convective wind damage associated with a microburst.

Snow slowly dissipated from west to east late in the evening on March 9th and into the early overnight on March 10th. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A rapidly strengthening storm developed across the Northern Plains and into the western Great Lakes on March 16-17. An initial band of precipitation developed during the early morning hours of March 16 across northwest Iowa in the form of light rain or light freezing rain. However, a sharp fall in temperatures by midday and early afternoon forced a change to a few hours of snowfall accompanied by increasing northerly wind. Snow cover prior to the event was limited to areas north of Highway 18, where impacts from snow and blowing snow with winds of 45 to 55 mph were greatest during the afternoon of March 16, and again briefly on Friday, March 17 when reinvigorated winds brought very brief visibility of a quarter mile or less.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief period of light freezing rain resulted in a glaze of icing, prior to a period of snowfall that accumulated to 0.5 inch at the COOP site at Sanborn. Northerly wind increased by the afternoon with gusts as high as 51 mph at Automated Weather Observing System site KSHL at Sheldon, resulting in very brief visibility reduction to around one mile.

Later in the day, a deepening low across the central plains lifted into Iowa with storms developing along a dry line in the evening. These storms produced hail up to baseball sized, along with a brief tornado remained rural and did not cause any damage. Additional convection was reinvigorated overnight thanks to the low level et, but remained sub severe. Areas that received multiple rounds of storms saw two to three inches of much needed rain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Early to mid April in Iowa was marked by exceptionally dry, warm, and breezy conditions. This resulted in several days of Red Flag Warning issuances across the area when relative humidity dropped under 25 percent, winds gusted over 30 mph, and much above average temperatures climbed into the low 80s. This resulted in a number of fires that became uncontrolled through the first half of the month. On April 13th, one fire resulted in an individual becoming severely burned.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: One person conducting a controlled burn was severely injured when the fire became uncontrolled. The fire quickly spread and engulfed the individual who was using a tractor to stop further spread of the fire.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough across the Rockies underwent lee cyclogenesis, pulling a warm front north into Iowa in the afternoon. While a few storms developed along the warm front, most development was along the later cold front that moved across the area in the evening. These storms were frequent hail producers, with many reports of baseball sized hail or larger. A tornado also occurred which resulted in damage to a few homes, out buildings, and trees.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Time estimated by radar.

A strong cold front crossed central Pennsylvania during the afternoon and early evening of April 1, 2023. In a high shear/low CAPE environment, convection was able to mix down very strong winds from just off the surface, leading to wind damage across portions of the area. Storms were weakening as they moved into central PA in the early afternoon, but they re-intensified over the Lower Susquehanna Valley by late afternoon and early evening. Winds following the frontal passage continued to gust to near 50 mph across southern Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing winds estimated near 60 mph knocked down trees along Route 6 east of Galeton.

These storms produced hail up to baseball sized, along with a brief tornado remained rural and did not cause any damage. Additional convection was reinvigorated overnight thanks to the low level et, but remained sub severe. Areas that received multiple rounds of storms saw two to three inches of much needed rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 24 hour rainfall report of 2.01 inches. Rain ongoing at time of report.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough across the Rockies underwent lee cyclogenesis, pulling a warm front north into Iowa in the afternoon. While a few storms developed along the warm front, most development was along the later cold front that moved across the area in the evening. These storms were frequent hail producers, with many reports of baseball sized hail or larger. A tornado also occurred which resulted in damage to a few homes, out buildings, and trees.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report via social media.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered showers and thunderstorms pushed into Pennsylvania from the south during the morning and afternoon of April 15, 2023, associated with upper-level low pressure approaching from the southern Appalachians. One storm that intensified over northern York County produced a brief funnel cloud. The funnel did not appear to touch down, and no damage was reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained NWS spotter observed a funnel cloud while traveling northbound on Route 15 near Clear Spring in northern York County. The funnel was observed near the intersection of York, Adams, and Cumberland counties. Pictures and video of the funnel show that it did not appear to touch down, and there was no reported damage in the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front crossed Pennsylvania during the afternoon of April 22, 2023, accompanied by showers and thunderstorms. In a low CAPE/moderate shear environment, the storms congealed into a north-south oriented line containing embedded bowing segments over the Susquehanna Valley and managed to produce sporadic wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing winds estimated near 60 mph tore half of the roof off of the Areba Barn on the Hershey Medical Center campus. A large piece of the roofing landed on a car, denting the car and breaking the rear window. There were also several trees down in a residential area across Route 322 from the Barn, along Hillview Lane and West Areba Drive.

An organized line of convection developed ahead of the cold front and created strong winds and isolated tornadoes from eastern Illinois to eastern Ohio. A wildfire developed during the afternoon hours of April 20, 2023 in Rush Township, Centre County during a stretch of unseasonably warm and dry weather. By mid-morning on April 21, the fire had grown to approximately 1200 acres. At the fire's peak, two fixed wing air tankers and a helicopter were enlisted to battle the fire, along with firefighting crews on the ground. Scattered rain showers and cooler temperatures from the evening of April 21 into April 22 helped firefighters to gain control of the fire.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wildfire developed during the afternoon of April 20, 2023 in Rush Township near the intersection of Sandy Ridge Trail and Ponderosa Drive. The wildfire occurred during a stretch of unseasonably warm and dry weather, and it quickly expanded in size to around 500 acres by evening. By mid-morning on April 21, the fire had grown to approximately 1200 acres. At the fire's peak, two fixed wing air tankers and a helicopter were enlisted to battle the fire, along with firefighting crews on the ground. Scattered rain showers and cooler temperatures from the evening of April 21 into April 22 helped firefighters to gain control of the fire.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Convection percolated along a warm front across the area through the morning. By afternoon, storms re-strengthened as as daytime heating helped enhance instability. Despite good instability with MLCAPE over nearing 2000 J/kg, lapse rates were modest and speed shear was weak. Despite this, directional shear was good and when combined with instability for brief stretching, allowed for a number of weak and short-lived tornadoes to develop. While 13 tornadoes occurred, they were confined to two small areas in Iowa where storms trained, resulting in several storms over the same locations. In addition, the training storms made for pockets of heavy rain with three to four inches or more of rain. This did result in flash flooding in Pocahontas County with impacts to homes and businesses.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Brief tornado reported by storm chaser southwest of Fonda. No damage indicators were impacted, therefore the EFU rating.

Despite good instability with MLCAPE over nearing 2000 J/kg, lapse rates were modest and speed shear was weak. Despite this, directional shear was good and when combined with instability for brief stretching, allowed for a number of weak and short-lived tornadoes to develop. While 13 tornadoes occurred, they were confined to two small areas in Iowa where storms trained, resulting in several storms over the same locations. In addition, the training storms made for pockets of heavy rain with three to four inches or more of rain. This did result in flash flooding in Pocahontas County with impacts to homes and businesses.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Brief tornado reported by storm chaser. No damage indicators were impacted, hence the EFU rating.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Convection began in early afternoon in eastern Iowa along a subtle boundary across the state. This was fueled by high CAPE exceeding 3000 J/kg with deep layer shear sufficient to support large hail growth. Later in the evening a secondary round of convection moved across the area producing additional hail in the form of a cold pool driven MCS, driven along the plume of higher instability. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very strong system developed on the morning of March 31st and tracked across the state of Iowa. This system pulled unseasonably warm and moist air into the Midwest, which combined with a very favorable wind profile to create a volatile environment for severe thunderstorms.  Discrete supercell thunderstorms occurred initially, but quickly transitioned into a QLCS mode. This system produced a historic tornado outbreak for the area, with a record 29 tornadoes on the day, including 13 rated EF-2, 1 rated EF-3, and 1 rated EF-4. This was the first EF-4 tornado in the NWS Quad Cities service area since 1995. 11 injuries were reported, with no known fatalities. In addition to the numerous tornadoes, there were many large hail and damaging wind reports. Maximum straight line thunderstorm winds were estimated at 80 to 90 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter reported that large trees were blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Deep moisture transport phased with an elongated trough across the central United States. The surface low quickly deepened across the central plains, bringing a variety of precipitation impacts to Iowa. Precipitation began as rain in southern Iowa with a transition to freezing rain as temperatures fell. Across northern Iowa, precipitation fell primarily as snow with totals of four to nine inches reported. Towards east central Iowa, lack of ice introduction aloft resulted in period of heavy sleet and freezing rain. At the same time, winds through the day gusted 35 to 45 mph across the entire state, causing drifting snow and significantly reducing visibility at times. Many locations reported a quarter up to a half inch of ice accumulation. Dozens of car accidents occurred as a result and many schools were closed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very strong system developed on the morning of March 31st and tracked across the state of Iowa. This system pulled unseasonably warm and moist air into the Midwest, which combined with a very favorable wind profile to create a volatile environment for severe thunderstorms.  Discrete supercell thunderstorms occurred initially, but quickly transitioned into a QLCS mode. This was the first EF-4 tornado in the NWS Quad Cities service area since 1995. 11 injuries were reported, with no known fatalities. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Convection percolated along a warm front across the area through the morning. By afternoon, storms re-strengthened as as daytime heating helped enhance instability. Despite good instability with MLCAPE over nearing 2000 J/kg, lapse rates were modest and speed shear was weak. Despite this, directional shear was good and when combined with instability for brief stretching, allowed for a number of weak and short-lived tornadoes to develop. While 13 tornadoes occurred, they were confined to two small areas in Iowa where storms trained, resulting in several storms over the same locations. In addition, the training storms made for pockets of heavy rain with three to four inches or more of rain. This did result in flash flooding in Pocahontas County with impacts to homes and businesses.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm Chaser has video of the weak tornado passing across rural portions of Warren county.  Some minor tree damage occurred.  This tornado then proceeded into Marion county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough lifted of of the four corners region and into the midwest, initially pulling a frontogenetical band of brief heavy snow across southern Iowa on the night of February 15th. This was fueled by high CAPE exceeding 3000 J/kg with deep layer shear sufficient to support large hail growth. Later in the evening a secondary round of convection moved across the area producing additional hail in the form of a cold pool driven MCS, driven along the plume of higher instability. The result was dozen of hail reports up to baseball sized across much of central and southern Iowa, damaging homes and vehicles and taking down power lines. As storms crossed Interstate 80 an accident resulted in significant delays.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Golf ball to baseball sized hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very strong system developed on the morning of March 31st and tracked across the state of Iowa. This system pulled unseasonably warm and moist air into the Midwest, which combined with a very favorable wind profile to create a volatile environment for severe thunderstorms.  Discrete supercell thunderstorms occurred initially, but quickly transitioned into a QLCS mode. This system produced a historic tornado outbreak for the area, with a record 29 tornadoes on the day, including 13 rated EF-2, 1 rated EF-3, and 1 rated EF-4. This was the first EF-4 tornado in the NWS Quad Cities service area since 1995. 11 injuries were reported, with no known fatalities. In addition to the numerous tornadoes, there were many large hail and damaging wind reports. Maximum straight line thunderstorm winds were estimated at 80 to 90 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter reported power lines and trees down at 32nd Street and Peru Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Convection percolated along a warm front across the area through the morning. By afternoon, storms re-strengthened as as daytime heating helped enhance instability. Despite good instability with MLCAPE over nearing 2000 J/kg, lapse rates were modest and speed shear was weak. Despite this, directional shear was good and when combined with instability for brief stretching, allowed for a number of weak and short-lived tornadoes to develop. While 13 tornadoes occurred, they were confined to two small areas in Iowa where storms trained, resulting in several storms over the same locations. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Deep moisture transport phased with an elongated trough across the central United States. The surface low quickly deepened across the central plains, bringing a variety of precipitation impacts to Iowa. Precipitation began as rain in southern Iowa with a transition to freezing rain as temperatures fell. Across northern Iowa, precipitation fell primarily as snow with totals of four to nine inches reported. Towards east central Iowa, lack of ice introduction aloft resulted in period of heavy sleet and freezing rain. At the same time, winds through the day gusted 35 to 45 mph across the entire state, causing drifting snow and significantly reducing visibility at times. Many locations reported a quarter up to a half inch of ice accumulation. Dozens of car accidents occurred as a result and many schools were closed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very strong system developed on the morning of March 31st and tracked across the state of Iowa. This system pulled unseasonably warm and moist air into the Midwest, which combined with a very favorable wind profile to create a volatile environment for severe thunderstorms.  Discrete supercell thunderstorms occurred initially, but quickly transitioned into a QLCS mode. This system produced a historic tornado outbreak for the area, with a record 29 tornadoes on the day, including 13 rated EF-2, 1 rated EF-3, and 1 rated EF-4. This was the first EF-4 tornado in the NWS Quad Cities service area since 1995. 11 injuries were reported, with no known fatalities. In addition to the numerous tornadoes, there were many large hail and damaging wind reports. Maximum straight line thunderstorm winds were estimated at 80 to 90 mph.

Convection began in early afternoon in eastern Iowa along a subtle boundary across the state. This was fueled by high CAPE exceeding 3000 J/kg with deep layer shear sufficient to support large hail growth. Later in the evening a secondary round of convection moved across the area producing additional hail in the form of a cold pool driven MCS, driven along the plume of higher instability. The result was dozen of hail reports up to baseball sized across much of central and southern Iowa, damaging homes and vehicles and taking down power lines. As storms crossed Interstate 80 an accident resulted in significant delays.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Spotter reported strong winds with potential damage and large hail with wide range of sizes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Deep moisture transport phased with an elongated trough across the central United States. The surface low quickly deepened across the central plains, bringing a variety of precipitation impacts to Iowa. Precipitation began as rain in southern Iowa with a transition to freezing rain as temperatures fell. Across northern Iowa, precipitation fell primarily as snow with totals of four to nine inches reported. Towards east central Iowa, lack of ice introduction aloft resulted in period of heavy sleet and freezing rain. At the same time, winds through the day gusted 35 to 45 mph across the entire state, causing drifting snow and significantly reducing visibility at times. Many locations reported a quarter up to a half inch of ice accumulation. Dozens of car accidents occurred as a result and many schools were closed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong winter storm brought moderate to heavy snow to portions of eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois late Friday night and early Saturday morning. Precipitation began as rain that quickly changed over to snow early Saturday.  Heavy wet snow fell east of a line from Fairfield, to Iowa City and Dubuque, and generally north of a line from Burlington, Iowa to Galesburg, Illinois.  The heaviest snowfall amounts between 8 and 12 inches fell from extreme eastern Iowa in Cedar, Scott, and Clinton counties, to Carroll, Jo Daviess, and Stephenson counties in Illinois.  This heavy snow caused numerous accidents and downed several tree branches due to the weight of the snow.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotters, Cocorahs, and numerous public reports showed 7 to 11.5 inches of heavy wet snow fell early in the morning March 25th. This heavy snow caused dangerous travel early in the day, and brought down numerous tree branches.  The most snow fell in northern Scott County.

Later in the evening a secondary round of convection moved across the area producing additional hail in the form of a cold pool driven MCS, driven along the plume of higher instability. The result was dozen of hail reports up to baseball sized across much of central and southern Iowa, damaging homes and vehicles and taking down power lines. As storms crossed Interstate 80 an accident resulted in significant delays.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Deep moisture transport phased with an elongated trough across the central United States. The surface low quickly deepened across the central plains, bringing a variety of precipitation impacts to Iowa. Precipitation began as rain in southern Iowa with a transition to freezing rain as temperatures fell. Across northern Iowa, precipitation fell primarily as snow with totals of four to nine inches reported. Towards east central Iowa, lack of ice introduction aloft resulted in period of heavy sleet and freezing rain. At the same time, winds through the day gusted 35 to 45 mph across the entire state, causing drifting snow and significantly reducing visibility at times. Many locations reported a quarter up to a half inch of ice accumulation. Dozens of car accidents occurred as a result and many schools were closed.

A very strong system developed on the morning of March 31st and tracked across the state of Iowa. This system pulled unseasonably warm and moist air into the Midwest, which combined with a very favorable wind profile to create a volatile environment for severe thunderstorms.  Discrete supercell thunderstorms occurred initially, but quickly transitioned into a QLCS mode. This system produced a historic tornado outbreak for the area, with a record 29 tornadoes on the day, including 13 rated EF-2, 1 rated EF-3, and 1 rated EF-4. This was the first EF-4 tornado in the NWS Quad Cities service area since 1995. 11 injuries were reported, with no known fatalities. In addition to the numerous tornadoes, there were many large hail and damaging wind reports. Maximum straight line thunderstorm winds were estimated at 80 to 90 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A review of Sentinel satellite data confirms that a separate tornado developed near Amish, and moved northeast around 6 miles to near Frytown, before dissipating. The tornado caused damage to farm outbuildings along its path. The tornado was rated EF0 with maximum winds around 85 mph. After the tornado dissipated, the associated supercell thunderstorm cycled again and produced an EF2 tornado that tracked from Coralville to Solon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough lifted of of the four corners region and into the midwest, initially pulling a frontogenetical band of brief heavy snow across southern Iowa on the night of February 15th. Behind this, isentropic lift with deep saturation and lift through the dendritic growth zone allowed for heavy snow rates through the day on February 16th. By later afternoon into early evening snow began to taper off from west to east, leaving behind a wide swath of seven to nine inches of snow across southern Iowa, generally along and south of the interstate 80 corridor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of heavy rain and anomalously warm temperatures melting a deeper than average snowpack during April resulted in third to fifth highest crests on record and moderate to major flooding at sites along the Upper Mississippi River in Iowa. Initial minor flood stage was reached in the middle of April with near record crests towards the end of April. In response to the flooding a Proclamation of Disaster Emergency was issued for counties along the Mississippi River by the Governor of Iowa. Drier conditions for the latter half of April and well below normal rainfall through May allowed the Upper Mississippi River to steadily recede, dropping below minor flood stage at sites along the Mississippi River in Iowa in the middle of May.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Significant upstream runoff from the combination of heavy rainfall and rapidly melting snow resulted in the third highest crest on record at the McGregor Dam towards the end of April. Subsequent dry conditions allowed the Mississippi River to slowly recede and drop below minor flood stage at the McGregor Dam on May 15th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense storm system tracked across the state of Iowa on Friday, March 31st. This system pulled unseasonably warm and moist conditions into the Midwest, which coupled with a very favorable wind profile and created quite the volatile environment for severe thunderstorms. This produced several long lived supercells which developed across central Iowa during the afternoon.  The storms were prolific hail producers along with a few reports of wind damage as they moved rapidly northeast.  Eventually, the storms produced a few tornadoes before exiting into eastern Iowa.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching frontal boundary generated widely scattered showers and thunderstorms in a low-CAPE/high shear environment during the afternoon and early evening of March 25, 2023. These storms dissipated as they progressed eastward from western Pennsylvania into a more stable, cold air dammed airmass over central Pennsylvania. However, Warren County was able to break into the warm sector briefly, and a sub-severe thunderstorm producing winds estimated near 50 mph pushed across the northern part of the county and knocked down a tree onto wires. Following the frontal passage, strong winds up to 50 mph buffeted the western highlands and caused sporadic damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm producing winds estimated near 50 mph knocked down a tree onto wires along PA Route 27 in Sugar Grove Township, closing the road.

However, Warren County was able to break into the warm sector briefly, and a sub-severe thunderstorm producing winds estimated near 50 mph pushed across the northern part of the county and knocked down a tree onto wires. Following the frontal passage, strong winds up to 50 mph buffeted the western highlands and caused sporadic damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong post-frontal winds estimated near 50 mph knocked down a tree onto a mobile home at 128 Double D Drive in Somerset Township, causing structural damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) and extreme (D3) drought conditions at the start of November remained constant across northeast Iowa through November from long-standing abnormally dry conditions. While the previous month of October provided near to slightly above normal rainfall amounts, total rainfall near 20 inches from April 1 to October 31st was 9 to 12 inches below normal. During November, only 1 to 3 days of measurable precipitation provided 0.1 to 0.5 inches total rainfall, near 2 inches below the monthly normal. While the growing season was all but over, multiple days of above normal temperatures, 10 to 20 degrees above normal, inhibited the ground from freezing. The drought remained unchanged through November as county-encompassing extreme drought (D3) extended from Mitchell and Floyd counties eastward to Winneshiek and Fayette counties. Widespread severe drought (D2) continued in Allamakee and Clayton counties with areas of extreme drought (D3).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought persisted across all of Allamakee County through November. The combination of total monthly precipitation under 0.2 inches, more than 2 inches below normal in spots, and several days of anomalously warm temperatures resulted in 20 to 30% below normal topsoil moisture.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense storm system tracked across the state of Iowa on Friday, March 31st. This system pulled unseasonably warm and moist conditions into the Midwest, which coupled with a very favorable wind profile and created quite the volatile environment for severe thunderstorms. This produced several long lived supercells which developed across central Iowa during the afternoon.  The storms were prolific hail producers along with a few reports of wind damage as they moved rapidly northeast.  Eventually, the storms produced a few tornadoes before exiting into eastern Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail began around 250pm and lasted through 254pm CDT. Largest stones with one inch in diameter and accumulated on flat surfaces and in drifts due to strong south winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure moved up the Ohio Valley and passed over Pennsylvania March 3 into early on March 4, 2023. In the wake of this system, gusty west to northwest winds impacted the area. The winds were particularly strong across the Laurel Highlands and southern Alleghenies, where gusts approaching 60 mph were observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Northwesterly winds occasionally gusting to near 60 mph occurred for several hours in Blair County. The ASOS at Altoona Airport recorded a wind gust to 58 mph, as did a mesonet site near Martinsburg. As a result, there were numerous reports of trees and wires down across the county.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Long track tornado began in Wapello County northeast |of Ottumwa then tracked northeast into Keokuk County. |The primary damage in Wapello County consisted of three |homes and one hog confinement facility. The first home |lost the entire roof and one external wall. The first failure |point was likely the wind entering and lifting the garage |which then led to failure of the roof. The home only had |straight nailed connections to the external walls spaced|every 18 inches and less to the roof. An unoccupied |mobile home on the property was not well anchored and |rolled to total destruction. This location was rated 110 mph |and EF-1. Two well anchored hog confinement buildings |were totally destroyed and were rated EF-2. The tornado |then impacted a location with a well built 2 story brick |house. The house suffered some roof and window damage |and a loss of a garage door but sustained little other |damage. Other damage indicators at the site suggested |EF-1 winds. Total destruction of a house occurred just |prior to the tornado exiting the county. This older house |sat unanchored to the concrete block basement. The house |was pushed off the foundation and crumbled. Some trees |near the house and a propane tank were mostly left with |little damage. A larger tree directly next to the house on |the wind side had several large limbs removed. Due to |all of these reasons, the wind at this location has been |rated at 135 mph, or high end EF-2.

Amounts decreased rapidly on either side of this narrow swath of heavier snow.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A quick-hitting winter storm produced a 8 to 10 inches of snow across all but far northern Potter County in less than 12 hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure tracked out of the Ohio Valley and through the southern Great Lakes on March 10th, passing just south of Erie, PA during the afternoon hours. A swath of accumulating snow occurred to the north of this low pressure, with a narrow band of heavy snow impacting extreme northwest Pennsylvania from late in the morning through much of the afternoon. Snow rates exceeded one inch per hour at times in this band of heavy snow. A trained spotter recorded a peak snowfall of 10.5 inches with this storm in North East Township. Elsewhere, a spotter measured 10 inches in Greene Township and 9.5 inches in Greenfield Township. Observers at Erie International Airport reported 6.1 inches of snow with this storm. Traffic accidents resulted, including a multi-vehicle accident along I-90 at mile marker 39 outside of North East Township. This accident closed I-90 Eastbound for several hours.

The strongest storms produced severe hail ranging from 1.0 to 1.5 inches in diameter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail 1.5 inches in diameter fell in Doon.

The combination of heavy rain and anomalously warm temperatures melting a deeper than average snowpack during April resulted in third to fifth highest crests on record and moderate to major flooding at sites along the Upper Mississippi River in Iowa. Initial minor flood stage was reached in the middle of April with near record crests towards the end of April. In response to the flooding a Proclamation of Disaster Emergency was issued for counties along the Mississippi River by the Governor of Iowa. Drier conditions for the latter half of April and well below normal rainfall through May allowed the Upper Mississippi River to steadily recede, dropping below minor flood stage at sites along the Mississippi River in Iowa in the middle of May.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Significant upstream runoff from the combination of heavy rainfall and rapidly melting snow resulted in the fourth highest crest on record in Lansing towards the end of April. Subsequent dry conditions allowed the Mississippi River to slowly recede and drop below minor flood stage in Lansing on May 4th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Four consecutive days of light to heavy rainfall events during the middle of May resulted in near 1.5 inches and some minor flooding along the more narrow, shallow rivers in northeast Iowa. Initial light to moderate rainfall on May 12th quenched soils from a drier than normal spring, while subsequent storms over the weekend of May 13th-14th resulted in rapid runoff and minor flooding along the Little Cedar and Turkey Rivers. Along the Little Cedar River, the highest realized height above flood stage occurred in Nashua (Chickasaw County) on May 16th with 0.94 feet. Along the Turkey River, the river gauge in Cresco (Howard County) crested 0.57 feet above flood stage on May 15th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Significant runoff from heavy rainfall upstream resulted in a rapid rise of water and minor flooding along the Little Cedar River near Orchard on May 15th. Minor flooding was initially realized late on May 14th, with the river cresting 0.51 feet above flood stage of 1081.5 feet above sea level during the early morning of May 15th. It then fell below flood stage later that morning.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very strong system developed on the morning of March 31st and tracked across the state of Iowa. This system pulled unseasonably warm and moist air into the Midwest, which combined with a very favorable wind profile to create a volatile environment for severe thunderstorms.  Discrete supercell thunderstorms occurred initially, but quickly transitioned into a QLCS mode. This system produced a historic tornado outbreak for the area, with a record 29 tornadoes on the day, including 13 rated EF-2, 1 rated EF-3, and 1 rated EF-4. This was the first EF-4 tornado in the NWS Quad Cities service area since 1995. 11 injuries were reported, with no known fatalities. In addition to the numerous tornadoes, there were many large hail and damaging wind reports. Maximum straight line thunderstorm winds were estimated at 80 to 90 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Another large, violent tornado developed in eastern Keokuk County as the initial tornado was weakening southwest of Keota. The tornado tracked to the northeast, on the western fringe of Keota, and crossed into Washington County near the intersection of Keokuk-Washington Road and 180th St. The tornado then continued through northwest Washington county, extreme southeast Iowa County, and into far southwest Johnson County. The tornado severely damaged several homes near Keota, wiping one house completely off its foundation, resulting in EF-4 level damage. A car was lofted in the air and tossed about 1000 feet into a nearby field and trees were completely debarked with only stubs of the largest branches remaining. As the tornado tracked west of Wellman, Iowa it knocked over a 325 ft cell phone tower. The tornado began to dissipate as it tracked into far southwest Johnson County. The tornado was rated EF-4 in Keokuk County, EF-3 in Washington County, and EF-1 in Iowa and Johnson Counties.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low moved east-northeastward from southern Lake Michigan to Lake Ontario during the morning through early afternoon of April 1st. Simultaneously, the low's trailing cold front moved from the southwestern Great Lakes and Middle MS Valley toward central NY and the Upper OH Valley. Scattered multicell showers and thunderstorms persisted generally northeastward and eastward ahead of, along, and just behind the surface cold front during the wee hours of the 1st and again during the early afternoon of the 1st. These showers and storms encountered moderate to strong effective bulk shear, weak DCAPE, and weak MUCAPE that increased somewhat and transitioned from elevated to surface-based by late morning as the boundary layer destabilized via daytime heating. Despite the marginally-favorable thermodynamic environment, showers and storms generated sporadic damaging convective gusts during the wee hours of the 1st and again during the early afternoon of the 1st.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Meadville Airport ASOS recorded a peak gust of 58 mph from passing thunderstorm.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very strong system developed on the morning of March 31st and tracked across the state of Iowa. This system pulled unseasonably warm and moist air into the Midwest, which combined with a very favorable wind profile to create a volatile environment for severe thunderstorms.  Discrete supercell thunderstorms occurred initially, but quickly transitioned into a QLCS mode. This system produced a historic tornado outbreak for the area, with a record 29 tornadoes on the day, including 13 rated EF-2, 1 rated EF-3, and 1 rated EF-4. This was the first EF-4 tornado in the NWS Quad Cities service area since 1995. 11 injuries were reported, with no known fatalities. In addition to the numerous tornadoes, there were many large hail and damaging wind reports. Maximum straight line thunderstorm winds were estimated at 80 to 90 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado developed just southwest of Coralville, crossed Highway 218 and damaged the James St. Warehouse near Highway 6 in Coralville. Several trailers and a truck were flipped over in the vicinity. A retail building also had part of a roof lifted off with several vehicles rolled or flipped. The tornado then tracked into a residential area and uprooted and snapped numerous trees. At least 2 injuries were reported by emergency management. Damage then became more sporadic before the tornado reintensified across Coralville Reservoir. A more concentrated path began near Sugar Bottom campground east of North Liberty and continued northeast towards Solon. A radio tower collapsed and a roof was lifted off a home and partially removed. The tornado continued northeast into a field before eventually reaching another farmstead and destroying an outbuilding. Debris from the farmstead was lofted into a field with a 2x4 driven into the ground. The tornado continued into Solon, uprooting trees, bending street signs, and destroying another outbuilding before dissipating and lifting just north of Sutliff Rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weakening upper level low pressure area moved into far southeast South Dakota by early evening. Slow moving thunderstorms developed within a very narrow axis which nosed into Buena Vista County, where the environment featured maximized and collocated 0-3km shear and 0-3km CAPE, and resulted in a few brief tornadoes connected with storm development phase.  In addition, very efficient thermodynamic profiles resulted in extremely heavy rainfall rates, with observed rates up to 2 to 3 inches per hour.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado spun up just north of the Sac-Buena Vista County border between 90th and 100th Avenue. The circulation featured intermittent contact with the surface for the next mile, as the tornado tracked a bit more westward after crossing 90th Avenue. There were no damage indicators impacted along the track, which was documented fully on storm chaser video. An EF rating could not be determined and the average path width was estimated to be 50 yards.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very strong system developed on the morning of March 31st and tracked across the state of Iowa. This system pulled unseasonably warm and moist air into the Midwest, which combined with a very favorable wind profile to create a volatile environment for severe thunderstorms.  Discrete supercell thunderstorms occurred initially, but quickly transitioned into a QLCS mode. This system produced a historic tornado outbreak for the area, with a record 29 tornadoes on the day, including 13 rated EF-2, 1 rated EF-3, and 1 rated EF-4. This was the first EF-4 tornado in the NWS Quad Cities service area since 1995. 11 injuries were reported, with no known fatalities. In addition to the numerous tornadoes, there were many large hail and damaging wind reports. Maximum straight line thunderstorm winds were estimated at 80 to 90 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado touched down just south of Bellevue, and moved northeast over the Mississippi River before dissipating. This tornado impacted an RV park and some cabins located nearby. Some structural damage was noted, with some RVs that were flipped and damaged. Several trees within the area were also impacted, with some uprooted. Three  injuries were noted with this tornado in the vicinity of the RV park. This tornado continued into Jo Daviess County, Illinois, but likely dissipated over the river as no damage was observed in a wooded area adjacent to the river. Peak winds were estimated around 105 mph.

The tornado continued to track to the northeast through a rural area, causing sporadic tree damage.  The tornado entered extreme northwest Scott County about a third of a mile south of 220th St., then travelled around one mile before entering Clinton County about a half mile west of the intersection of 280th St. and 110th Ave. The tornado then dissipated about 2 miles south of Wheatland. The peak winds were estimated at 120 mph. The tornado was rated EF-2 in Cedar County, and EF-0 in Scott and Clinton Counties.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In semi similar fashion to the strong and severe storms experienced on the previous morning (29th of June), storms initiated over portions of northern Kansas and southern Nebraska in conjunction with the low level jet in the very early hours of the 29th. These storms, steered by easterly mean flow, progressed across far southern Iowa and northern Missouri within an environment consisting of around 2000 J/kg MUCAPE, 30 to 40+ kts of effective shear, and a very tight north-south gradient of DCAPE (most favorably into Missouri). Storms grew upscale through the early morning hours and primarily produced strong and damaging winds. There were a couple of severe hail reports as well along with a reported lightning strike that effective blew a tree apart.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Law enforcement reported tree branch down on powerlines. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low moved east-northeastward from southern Lake Michigan to Lake Ontario during the morning through early afternoon of April 1st. Simultaneously, the low's trailing cold front moved from the southwestern Great Lakes and Middle MS Valley toward central NY and the Upper OH Valley. Scattered multicell showers and thunderstorms persisted generally northeastward and eastward ahead of, along, and just behind the surface cold front during the wee hours of the 1st and again during the early afternoon of the 1st. These showers and storms encountered moderate to strong effective bulk shear, weak DCAPE, and weak MUCAPE that increased somewhat and transitioned from elevated to surface-based by late morning as the boundary layer destabilized via daytime heating. Despite the marginally-favorable thermodynamic environment, showers and storms generated sporadic damaging convective gusts during the wee hours of the 1st and again during the early afternoon of the 1st.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree was downed onto parked car in Erie, near the zoo. Report did not state whether car was damaged.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective vortex (MCV) moved out of Nebraska and South Dakota, into Iowa in the afternoon of June 17th. Increased forcing with the MCV met with increasing instability as CAPE reach 1500-2000 J/kg in the afternoon. Storms developed quickly in a line, with a few isolated cells remaining on the southern end of the line. While deep shear was only around 25 kts, this was enough to sustain updraft capable of producing severe hail. Several locations in southwest Iowa reported quarter sized hail with one instance of thunderstorm wind damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In semi similar fashion to the strong and severe storms experienced on the previous morning (29th of June), storms initiated over portions of northern Kansas and southern Nebraska in conjunction with the low level jet in the very early hours of the 29th. These storms, steered by easterly mean flow, progressed across far southern Iowa and northern Missouri within an environment consisting of around 2000 J/kg MUCAPE, 30 to 40+ kts of effective shear, and a very tight north-south gradient of DCAPE (most favorably into Missouri). Storms grew upscale through the early morning hours and primarily produced strong and damaging winds. There were a couple of severe hail reports as well along with a reported lightning strike that effective blew a tree apart.

After a brief decrease in intensity entering Iowa, storms strengthened once again mid to late evening moving east of Cherokee generally along and south of Iowa Highway 3 with a variety of severe weather types.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A power pole along 80th Avenue just south of Iowa Highway 3 was leaning, nearby corn was flattened, and large tree branches were broken due to thunderstorm winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms ahead of a strong cold front developed and moved through the region. Storms produced gusty winds, small to medium sized hail, and a tornado in Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado began less than a mile southwest of Womelsdorf along PA Route 419 between Memorial Boulevard and Brickplant Road just over the Berks and Lebanon County line where a few old wooden telephone poles were pushed over. The tornado continued northeast through a field toward the Conrad Weiser West Elementary School. A few softwood trees in a tree line were snapped or uprooted along the property line of the field and the school. This is the location where the tornado reached its maximum estimated winds of 90 mph and maximum width of approximately 125 yards. The tornado continued across the school grounds and into a recreational field where a set |of metal bleachers was blown over. The tornado then moved northeast into the central part of Womelsdorf where varying degrees of minor damage occurred to structures and trees, mainly between 3rd Street and 2nd Street as the tornado crossed Cherry Alley, High Street, Mulberry Alley, and Franklin Street. Several homes, garages, and |barns had roofing material blow off, several small trees were uprooted, and numerous downed large tree branches caused some collateral structural damage to some homes and vehicles. The tornadic circulation began to weaken considerably as it crossed 2nd |Street north of Franklin Street near Pear Alley where some additional minor tree damage occurred. The tornado dissipated as it moved into the Womelsdorf Union Cemetery.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In semi similar fashion to the strong and severe storms experienced on the previous morning (29th of June), storms initiated over portions of northern Kansas and southern Nebraska in conjunction with the low level jet in the very early hours of the 29th. These storms, steered by easterly mean flow, progressed across far southern Iowa and northern Missouri within an environment consisting of around 2000 J/kg MUCAPE, 30 to 40+ kts of effective shear, and a very tight north-south gradient of DCAPE (most favorably into Missouri). Storms grew upscale through the early morning hours and primarily produced strong and damaging winds. There were a couple of severe hail reports as well along with a reported lightning strike that effective blew a tree apart.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: House fire started by lightning strike. The home experienced significant damage to the roof and upper floor. Time matched to CG lightning data.

Another storm cluster moved through the Quad Cities, producing wind gusts to 70 mph at the Davenport ASOS and damage to trees and power poles.  An EF-0 tornado also tracked east along and north of I-80 near the Davenport Airport, causing sporadic minor tree and structure damage.  This storm impacted the Quad City Airshow grounds, while no visitors were present.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On Thursday, June 29, a powerful severe wind event moved over the region. This event was known as a derecho given its long duration from north of Kansas City to southern Indiana and its consistent strong intensity. Almost all of the damage in the area surveyed locally was due to straight-line winds, at times easily peaking between 100-120 mph in far western Illinois. Those who experienced the event conveyed how the strongest winds persisted for 10 to 15 minutes, and in some locations, it lasted as long as 20 minutes, which is atypical for derecho events.||There were some swaths of enhanced damage. These were largely due to intense wind surges in the local area. One of these in Clark county, Mo was determined to be a short-lived EF1 tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power out, with 3 trees blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective vortex (MCV) moved out of Nebraska and South Dakota, into Iowa in the afternoon of June 17th. Increased forcing with the MCV met with increasing instability as CAPE reach 1500-2000 J/kg in the afternoon. Storms developed quickly in a line, with a few isolated cells remaining on the southern end of the line. While deep shear was only around 25 kts, this was enough to sustain updraft capable of producing severe hail. Several locations in southwest Iowa reported quarter sized hail with one instance of thunderstorm wind damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system slowly dropping SE form the eastern Dakotas and SW Minnesota dragged a cold front across the state during the evening and overnight hours of the 24th of June. Within the warm sector, MUCAPE values peaked in excess of 3000 J/kg during peak heating and scaled back a bit overnight but remained around or in excess of 2000 J/kg. Effective shear values were supportive for organized convection, residing in the 35 to around 50 kt range. Morning and lingering convective activity likely played a role in initiating some storms with remnant outflow boundaries around. The largest hail reported was 3 inches in both Palo Alto and Black Hawk counties. A couple of funnel clouds were reported as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public reported 1 inch hail, relayed from NWS Chat.
